items.title: Inspector Omogbai: Doing policing with motherly love
items.description: By Adesina Wahab She got enlisted in the Nigeria Police Force, NPF, 24 years ago and has risen through the ranks to become an Inspector in the Traffic Department. Justina Omogbai, a mother of five, was recently recognized and honoured by the management of Trinity University, Sabo, Yaba, Lagos during their second Registry Week and Lecture. They gave her a Certificate of Recognition and an undisclosed amount of money for her tireless efforts at ensuring students in public schools in that axis get to school on time and are properly dressed. Read Also: 25 children from Kebbi, Kwara, Niger died in terrorists’ captivity — Lawmaker After observing that some students are fond of loitering around when they ought to be in school, Omogbai turned herself to a chief whip, ensuring that they get to school early enough for their studies. Like a football referee, she would put a whistle in her mouth and clutch a cane, not to beat any student, but to scare them to do the right thing – get to school early enough. She has also become a Madam Santa Claus to some of the students she assists occasionally with writing materials, shoes, uniforms among others. To know the depth of the sacrifices she makes, one needs to have an idea of how much a police inspector earns monthly in the country. According to the Consolidated Police Salary Structure, CONPOSS, an Inspector of Police in Nigeria earns an estimated monthly basic salary between N167,000 and N254,000, depending on their precise sub-rank and grade level. The Inspector rank is divided into sub-categories which dictate the exact take-home pay: Inspector of Police (IP) II: N67,000 per month, Inspector of Police (IP) I: N254,000 per month. On what prompted her service to humanity, she said, “I was posted to Sabo, Yaba in 2021 and I have been in the service for 24 years. Everywhere I have worked in Lagos, I have always tried to distinguish myself. These pupils and students are our future leaders and we must do everything possible to lead them aright. They can be governors, President, Ministers or anything God has purposed for them in the future. Whenever I see them pass by without dressing properly, I feel for them. I also went to a public school and our parents took great care of us. We wore Cortina shoes to school and dressed well. Nobody wore slippers to school. “But now, some children don’t dress well to school, they will wear torn uniforms or not minding to wash those uniforms. And they go to school very late too. You will see a child that is supposed to be in school by 7.45am just strolling there by 8.30am or even 9am. Majority of them I see at food vendors’ places, or where they would meet to discuss sports and other issues. So, I said what kind of life is this? Because a wayward child today possibly started like that. So, I decided to take it upon myself to start to caution them. That they should not do such things but to have focus in life.” But with five children of her own, and with the current economic situation in the country, surely it is an arduous task living comfortably, not to think of serving in loco parentis to some children one does not know their parents. But Omogbai would not be deterred. She has kind words for her husband, an Air Force personnel for being her pillar of support. “It was difficult for me when I started, some of my colleagues were telling me whether I have taken adequate care of my own children. I have five children. When I talk to those children, I will draw them close and advise them. “There are 10 public schools in this axis that I take care of their students. Some of them do come to me to seek advice on issues or tell me what they are going through at home or in school. I do encourage them. I used to tell them that though I am not their biological mother, I am still a mother figure to them. Whenever I collect my salary, I used to dedicate part of it to their welfare. I buy socks, shoes, writing materials etc for them. I am glad that my husband also supports me, as without his support, I won’t be able to do those things.” Is she not behaving like a dog which wants to keep guard in two different apartments? Will one duty, precisely, her official duty, not suffer neglect, since she has turned herself to a timekeeper for the students? Explaining, she said she found a way of not letting her zeal for community work stand in the way of her official duty. “As a traffic officer, when I get to my point of duty, I will control the traffic to ensure free flow. Also, there are other officers with me including LASTMA people. After ensuring that the traffic is flowing, then I can move down to begin to look out for where the children normally stay to loiter. I have my whistle and I will blow it. Once I do that, the students will begin to run and move in the directions of their schools. Though I used to carry I cane, I never used it. The children fear me and when they hear the whistle, they know it is me and will do the right thing by heading to their schools.” With the thinking in some quarters that discipline has taken flight from our schools, the police inspector emphatised with teachers, expressing the feeling that they are surely overwhelmed with the number of students they cater to and handle. As a law officer and a mother, one would expect her to have a tough approach to raising children, but Omogbai believes that raising children is not all about shouting or beating them, “but talk to them like a parent and they will understand.” In the course of her community voluntary work, she said there has not been any reason to recommend taking any of the students to a remand home. “If they have issues with their teachers or school authorities , I do intervene and help to settle such,” she stated. On the part her background plays in her attitude to life, she noted her desire has been to positively impact others anytime and anywhere she goes. “I was born and raised in the barracks, the Air Force Base and I am married to an Air Force personnel. I want to make a difference in the lives of people, children, widows and anybody who comes my way and I am in the position to help. I never knew people were watching me. All of a sudden, somebody just told me they needed my attention at Trinity University and I asked whether I have done anything wrong and he said no, that they saw my good works and truly I enjoy doing the work. When you do good, God has a way of rewarding you. I am overwhelmed with the recognition given me by Trinity University. You could see that I was unable to talk, I shed tears of joy. I just started thanking God.” The motherly Police Inspector had encomium poured on her by the Vice Chancellor of Trinity University, Prof. Clement Kolawole and the Registrar, Mr David Oyejide, who described her as a positive influence on the young ones, who could learn the art of kindness and assisting others from her. Omogbai, who has received recognitions and has been honoured by different groups and individuals, is an example of proving wrong those who don’t believe that nothing good can come out of Nazareth of the Nigeria Police Force. The post Inspector Omogbai: Doing policing with motherly love appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Trump's attack on 'birth tourism' faces uphill legal battle after Supreme Court ruling
items.description: When the United States supreme court in June ruled in favour of broad citizenship rights for babies born in the country, one of the most conservative justices complained that the decision was so sweeping it would even cover so-called birth tourists. Women “who come here solely for the purpose of giving birth” would be able to get automatic citizenship for their children, Samuel Alito wrote, dissenting from the 6-3 ruling that invalidated President Donald Trump’s first attempt to curtail US birthright citizenship . Undeterred by the court’s ruling, Trump tried again on Thursday, signing two executive orders largely aimed at birth tourism. That part of Trump’s action, which is certain to face legal challenges, is likely doomed, legal experts said. It targets a category of people that legal experts said the supreme court already addressed. “These children are citizens based on their birth on US soil,” said University of Virginia law professor Amanda Frost, who studies birthright citizenship. “Illegal conduct by their parent can have no bearing on their status.” The Republican president has for years threatened to tighten birthright citizenship as part of his restrictive immigration agenda. On the first day of his second term in January 2025, Trump issued a sweeping order that targeted immigrants in the country illegally or even temporarily on a legal basis, including those on work visas or students. The court’s June 30 ruling striking it down, in a case called Trump v Barbara, held that the policy violated language in the US Constitution’s 14th Amendment that confers citizenship to those born in the United States who are “subject to the jurisdiction thereof”. To curtail birth tourism, one of Trump’s new orders directs federal agencies not to recognise a child’s citizenship if either parent is “engaged in fraudulent activity to obtain citizenship”. A second executive order seeks to bar visas for foreigners suspected of birth tourism, although it was unclear how it would be enforced. Federal regulation currently bars using temporary visas for the purpose of obtaining US citizenship for a newborn. Speaking in the Oval Office on Thursday, Trump renewed his criticism of the ruling and said that “people are building businesses around” birth tourism, suggesting that “hundreds of thousands” are wrongly benefiting. Some analyses cite smaller numbers, with Penn State University scholars estimating 5,000 to 10,000 births each year from 2014 to 2024. Besides birth tourism, Trump’s new directive also seeks to expand historical exceptions to automatic birthright citizenship, which include children of diplomatic representatives such as ambassadors and hostile foreign troops occupying US territory. The order would widen the categories to include foreign government employees and those deemed foreign terrorists. Scholars divided Scholars were divided over whether courts might allow some of these expansions. Expanding the category of diplomats is potentially legal, depending on how it is done, said Frost, “though that requires giving those people significant immunity from US law”. University of California, Berkeley law professor John Yoo, who worked as a Justice Department official during Republican George W Bush’s presidency, said that the order’s attempt to define foreign enemy forces on US soil as including terrorist organisations “will eventually pass constitutional muster.” Others said certain expansions may stretch too far. “Japanese immigrants to the US were deemed enemy aliens during World War II,” said University of Michigan law professor Sam Erman. “Under the administration’s rule, their US-born children could have been denied citizenship.” The legality of the various provisions could also depend on how agencies implement them. Some of the terms are elastic, such as the definition of an “alien enemy,” or the “purpose” of a stay, said Hiroshi Motomura, an immigration law expert at the University of California, Los Angeles. This creates “huge zones of discretion that allow officials of the US government to deny visas or admission based on suspicions or a need to vet further,” Motomura said. Court ruling The supreme court in June struck down Trump’s prior order, even though the administration argued that automatic birthright citizenship encourages illegal immigration and birth tourism. “Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights to freely participate in our political community,” Chief Justice Roberts wrote, adding that the authors of the 14th Amendment extended that promise to every free-born person in the land. “We keep that promise today,” Roberts wrote. Alito did not mince words in his dissent. “In my judgment, the court has made a mistake that will seriously affect the country’s future,” he wrote. He faulted the court for ruling that “even a child born to a mother who is here for only a brief time is a citizen under the Fourteenth Amendment”. Such a view yields “grotesque results,” Alito said. “While foreigners who wish to immigrate lawfully must sometimes wait for many years, a child born here to a birth tourist is automatically a citizen,” he said. White House aides defended the orders on Thursday. “There’s absolutely nothing in here that runs afoul of any of the supreme court’s opinions on the subject,“ White House Staff Secretary Will Scharf said. Yoo disagreed. “I do not see any exception to birthright, as defined by the court in Barbara, that would include parents who fraudulently violated federal law to give birth to children on American territory,” he said. Rachel Rosenbloom, an immigration law professor at Northeastern University, said she would be surprised if the order’s new exclusions survived a legal challenge, calling them “clearly unconstitutional.” “This order seems like a desperate measure by a president who is having a hard time accepting that he just suffered a significant loss at the supreme court,” Rosenbloom said.

items.title: Imo 2027: Can Uzodimma break 27-year-old jinx?
items.description: By Emmanuel Iheaka SINCE the return to democracy in 1999, no governor of Imo State has produced a successor. The first governor of the state in the current republic, Chief Achike Udenwa, failed to install a successor at the end of his two-term of eight years in 2007. Successive governors of the state have emerged through either what could be described as ballot revolution or powers from above. By the time the dust of the 2007 governorship election in the state settled, Chief Ikedi Ohakim of the now defunct Progressive Peoples Alliance, PPA, had been declared the new helmsman of Imo. Ohakim would later be ousted in 2011, in what could be described as one of the biggest political upsets in the current republic in the state. Eccentric Rochas Okorocha led a people-centred movement to displace Ohakim. But again, Okorocha failed to install a successor, when what majority saw as a selfish bid to crown his son in-law, came crumbling like a pack of cards. Former Speaker, House of Representatives, Chief Emeka Ihedioha, had the shortest stay on the governorship saddle of the state, following his sack by the Supreme Court, which paved the way for the incumbent, Senator Hope Uzodimma. Can Uzodimma break the jinx by producing a successor? Time will tell. However, there are early indications that the opposition will literally be fighting the battle of their life in the bid to maintain the history of the state, in not allowing any governor to produce a successor. Though the state government and the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC, have distanced themselves, the early attacks on opposition parties leave no one in doubt that it is not going to be a walk in the park for those opposing the APC. Pre-poll violence About a week ago, thugs reportedly disrupted a meeting of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, in Owerri Municipal, in which a Senatorial candidate of the party, Uche Onyeagucha, was addressing party members. Few days after the incident, the Young Progressives Party, YPP, and the All Peoples Party, APP, reported an attempt to break into their secretariats and destruction of their billboards at about midnight. The Imo State Chairman of YPP, Michael Anyanwu, said he got a distress call at about 3:00am on the fateful day, alerting him of the attack. Anyanwu vowed that his party would fight on. “I got a distress call by security guards on ground that between the hours of 3 and 4am, some unidentified men in an unmarked Sienna vehicle came to our party secretariat, vandalised our signages and wanted to make entry into the party secretariat, if not that our security guards had to create panic alert which made them to disperse. “This is not campaign signage, this is just to show landmark. I wonder why we will be targeted. Are they trying to silence opposition parties in Imo State? “I have gone to the police to make an entry. We are law-abiding party; we are not going to be cowed by anybody”, the chairman submitted. Attack stage-managed – APC The ruling APC has dismissed the said attack as stage-managed, and warned the opposition to play by the rules. In a statement, the state Publicity Secretary of the APC, Onwuasoanya Jones, said there were indications that the purported attack might have been stage-managed. APC stated that it is not threatened by the existence of any opposition party in the state and urged the opposition to play by the rules. “The All Progressives Congress in Imo State is not threatened by the existence of any political Party and would not go outside the law and established democratic methods in ensuring that we maintain our unassailable popularity and acceptability with Imo people. “Our Party frowns at any act of violence and disorderly behaviour and we encourage all opposition parties in the state to play by the rules by working towards convincing Imolites with logical arguments and verifiable records about why their parties might deserve the consideration of Imo people, rather than resorting to crude and unlawful strategies in order to draw attention. “While these parties might consider this as Disruptive Advertising or Marketing strategy, we must warn them to ensure that they follow the law in carrying out their activities and marketing their political parties to the populace, as any attempt to disturb the peace of the state or cause panic will be reported to the appropriate authorities for necessary investigations and actions”, the party had submitted. Speaking to Vanguard, APP which has become a major opposition party in the state, however, appears unperturbed and unruffled. Cajetan Duke, former Publicity Secretary of the party in Imo, and now the Chief Press Secretary to the leader of the party, Chima Amadi, insisted that APC is exit-bound in the state. According to Duke, the recent actions of the APC follow the known last minute pattern of actions of previously ousted ruling parties in the state. “APP has demonstrated enough readiness for the 2027 general elections in Imo. APC is aware that APP is the party to beat in Imo. APP is now the largest number one opposition party in Imo. We have two National Assembly members. That’s an indication of strength and acceptability. “What is happening in Imo has become a panic-reaction pattern by governments. In 2011, the PDP government was very hostile to Imo people because they realised the people had rejected them, to the point the government prevented APGA from holding a rally at the stadium. At a time, Rochas had to hold the rally on the streets of Owerri. What was the resultant effect of it, the people spoke through the ballot. Panic mood “In 2019, the outgoing government went into that panic mood and became hostile to the opposition. When they realised the people had left them, they decided to weaponise the government against the opposition. At the end of the day, the people stood their ground. “Today, the APC in Imo knows that the 2027 election is about the people trying to take back their destiny in their hands. The people are looking for credible alternatives and they have found that in APP. “You cannot intimidate people who have made up their minds. We have seen governments come and go. We know the behavioural tendencies of a government that is exit-bound. Imo people should remain resolute and law abiding. The darkest part of the night is the hour next to dawn. Guard your PVC, our votes will count”. Another major opposition party in the state, the African Democratic Congress, ADC, told Vanguard that it was battle-ready for the APC. State Publicity Secretary of the party, Macdonald Amadi, claimed that ADC has captured the nooks and crannies of the state . “My party has come to save Nigeria from hunger and starvation; provide basic health, quality education, and infrastructure. Our party is rooted in rule of law, and abhors violence and election rigging. “If there is any party that is prepared to rule in Imo, it is ADC. Our party has sold itself to the people of Imo in all the nooks and crannies of the state. We are ready for the 2027 general elections. “Our party is against blackmail and running down individuals. ADC believes in constructive criticism and holding governments accountable by getting them to pursue policies aimed at ensuring the welfare of the people.” Uzodimma’s scorecard There is a seeming consensus that the Uzodimma administration has done well in road construction and rescuing the state to a large extent, from the insecurity that ravaged it for years. But not a few point to the apparent neglect of the education sector, with many school buildings in decrepit condition. There is also what analysts describe as the disconnect between Uzodimma and the people, owing to what they term the governor’s elitist disposition. The APP led by the energetic Chima Amadi, and House of Representatives member, Ikenga Ugochinyere, has been vociferous in its criticism of the Uzodimma administration. The ADC, led by Emeka Ihedioha, has however, not been that loud. The surprising appearance of the erstwhile House of Representatives Speaker at the recent celebration of Imo at 50, where he received an award from Uzodimma, had sparked speculations and permutations about the 2027 political intrigues. The NDC doesn’t seem to have a definite governor aspirant at the moment. But one can easily guess that the former Chairman of the Nigeria Electricity Regulatory Commission, Dr. Sam Amadi, will fill in the gap. Whatever be the case, the forthcoming 2027 off-circle governorship election in Imo will be a clash of the titans that will either rewrite or retain the political history of the state. The post Imo 2027: Can Uzodimma break 27-year-old jinx? appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: US court orders halt to White House ballroom construction; Trump reacts
items.description: An appeals court on Friday upheld an order halting work on Donald Trump’s prized White House ballroom, enraging the US leader and setting up another Supreme Court battle over the limits of presidential authority. The US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit, which had allowed construction to continue while it considered the case, agreed with a lower court that such a massive White House overhaul required the explicit consent of Congress. It stayed its own decision for two weeks to give Trump time to ask the Supreme Court to intervene. The Republican president lashed out after the 2-1 ruling, calling it “horrendous, politically motivated, and unlawful.” The two judges in the majority were appointed by Democratic presidents, while the dissenter was nominated by Trump himself. The president vowed in a lengthy social media post to immediately appeal to the Supreme Court. “This decision, made after much of the work has been done and paid for, is a National Security Threat at the highest level. It is also a National Disgrace,” Trump said in another post on his Truth Social platform Friday night. Trump initially touted the construction of the ballroom as being necessary to host galas, but has since repeatedly pointed to the concurrent addition of an underground military bunker and other security features. – East Wing – Under the district judge’s initial order, work was to be allowed to continue only on a limited set of structures, including those that were underground. “This holding has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy. This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom,” the majority wrote Friday. “What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court’s expeditious litigation without securing Congress’s authorization, as the Constitution and laws require.” Trump, who has repeatedly complained that the White House lacks sufficient space for grand galas such as state dinners, unilaterally ordered construction of the massive ballroom. Work on the project began last year with the sudden demolition of the White House’s entire historic East Wing. Since then, photos have shown significant work on a basement complex, with some concrete walls rising up above ground. Trump has insisted that the ballroom will be privately financed, but media reports in June showed that significant taxpayer funds were going to the project, which could cost as much as $600 million. While the White House initially cited a $200 million price tag for the project, it quickly doubled the estimate to $400 million. The ballroom is just one of Trump’s pet projects to leave his mark on Washington by the time he leaves office in 2029, along with a renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and other parks, as well as the construction of a gigantic arch. Several of the projects have similarly faced legal challenges, but the ballroom project would be the first to reach the Supreme Court. AFP The post US court orders halt to White House ballroom construction; Trump reacts appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Salvation in the bus!, by Stephanie Shaakaa
items.description: There is a peculiar talent that governments sometimes acquire after years in office. It is the ability to mistake the symptom for the disease, to become so captivated by the manageable inconvenience that the genuine emergency fades into the wallpaper. Nations reveal themselves not only by the crises they endure, but by the crises they choose to confront. Some spend decades strengthening schools, courts and hospitals because they understand that institutions outlive administrations. Others become fascinated by the theatre of governance, where visible action is mistaken for meaningful progress. The recent controversy surrounding the Federal Road Safety Corps amendment bill and its provision on preaching, hawking and trading inside commercial vehicles belongs to that familiar theatre. Whether the clause merely restated an existing prohibition or represented a fresh legislative impulse is almost incidental. The real story was never a preacher standing in the aisle of a commercial bus. It was our astonishing ability to invest enormous public energy in a question that sits comfortably on the margins while the centre continues to collapse. If anyone wishes to understand why that instinct has become so deeply Nigerian, they should spend a single morning inside a commercial bus. A woman climbs aboard carrying two bags of tomatoes. To everyone else, they are groceries waiting to become sales. To her, they are school fees, cough syrup, transport fare and, if the day is kind, a piece of meat in the evening pot. She settles into a cracked seat and instinctively draws the bags closer, knowing that tomatoes bruise almost as easily as profit. Around her sits a country held together by quiet endurance. An elderly man keeps opening a brown envelope to reassure himself that the hospital test results are still inside. Across from him, a university graduate studies the reflection on the dark screen of his phone, silently rehearsing answers for interviews that rarely become employment. A young mother rocks a sleepy child while calculating how long she can postpone buying another tin of infant formula. Beside the window, a mechanic with grease permanently worked into his fingernails sleeps with the heavy exhaustion of someone who has mistaken survival for rest. Nobody asks another passenger’s name. It is unnecessary. In a Nigerian commercial bus, introductions are a luxury. Everyone arrives carrying a private burden, and everyone leaves with it. The conductor slaps the body of the bus. “One more! One more!” It is the oldest fiction in public transportation. There is never one more. There are always four. The engine coughs awake and the bus joins the slow procession of a city already bargaining with itself. Hawkers drift effortlessly through the traffic selling bottled water, handkerchiefs, chargers and biscuits. Office workers weave between vehicles with the urgency of people who know that lateness in Nigeria is often punished more severely than incompetence. Somewhere ahead, a broken-down tanker has converted an ordinary road into a lesson in collective patience. Inside the bus, the country’s parliament is already in session. “My landlord says the rent is going up again.” “My son graduated two years ago. He’s still looking.” “Rice was cheaper last week.” No one raises a voice. Hardship rarely requires volume. It simply settles into the empty spaces between ordinary conversations. The woman with the tomatoes says nothing. She is occupied by a mathematics that no university teaches. If she sells everything before noon, she can restock tomorrow. If prices rise again, she will buy fewer baskets. If her youngest daughter’s cough refuses to disappear, medicine will compete with school fees. If nothing unexpected happens, and in Nigeria that is always the most expensive assumption, perhaps tomorrow will resemble today. Then the bus crashes into a pothole. The tomatoes lurch forward. She catches them before they spill into the aisle. The old man instinctively shields his envelope. The graduate grips his phone. For a brief moment, every passenger reaches for the one fragile thing that cannot afford to break. At the next junction, a man rises from the back seat with a small Bible in his hand. His faded blue shirt has survived too many washings to remember its original colour. He smiles, clears his throat and begins softly. “My brothers and sisters…” Half the passengers already know how the story will unfold. Some bow their heads. Others continue staring through the window. The conductor keeps demanding exact change with unwavering commitment. The preacher speaks quietly about gratitude, uncertain journeys and the dangerous confidence of believing tomorrow has already made promises to us. When he finishes, he thanks the passengers, returns to his seat and becomes anonymous once again. The bus moves on, carrying not merely commuters, but a republic in miniature. In Part Two, I’ll pivot from this bus journey to the deeper political argument, showing why the real issue was never the preacher at all, before ending with a much more haunting conclusion built around the tomato seller. I think that’s where this version can rise from excellent to genuinely memorable. The bus offers a useful education for anyone trying to understand the country’s political imagination. A visitor spending his first day in Nigeria would leave with a catalogue of obvious national anxieties. He would see roads that consume more hours than distance should permit. He would hear conversations shaped by inflation, unemployment, rising rents and shrinking purchasing power. He would notice that almost every passenger is carrying a calculation invisible to everyone else, forever adding, subtracting and postponing. He would reasonably conclude that these are the questions occupying the full attention of those entrusted with governing. Then he would discover that one of the loudest public arguments concerns what should happen when someone begins preaching before the conductor has finished collecting transport fare. The bewilderment would be understandable. No society should object to conversations about courtesy in shared public spaces. Commuters deserve peace if they want it. Those who preach, trade or entertain inside commercial vehicles should exercise consideration for people who may be carrying grief, exhaustion or simply a desire for silence. Civilised societies are built on mutual respect. But proportion matters. The measure of a government’s seriousness is not whether it can regulate the small inconveniences of everyday life. It is whether it can summon the imagination and discipline to confront the larger forces that make those inconveniences feel unbearable in the first place. The woman carrying tomatoes does not board that bus wondering whether someone might preach before she reaches her destination. She wonders whether she will sell enough before the afternoon heat softens the fruit. The graduate is not consumed by the possibility of an unsolicited sermon. He is wondering whether another week will pass without the telephone call that changes his life. The elderly man is thinking about test results, not public order. Their burdens are older than the debate. They will almost certainly outlive it. That is the danger of symbolic politics. It creates the reassuring appearance of movement while leaving reality stubbornly where it has always been. It is easier to regulate behaviour than to repair institutions, easier to draft another rule than to rebuild an economy, easier to police the visible than to confront the slow, patient failures that quietly shape a nation’s destiny. History is full of governments that became remarkably efficient at organising appearances while neglecting foundations. They announced campaigns as factories closed. They enforced order as public confidence dissolved. They perfected the language of action while ordinary people perfected the art of endurance. Nigeria has never lacked regulations. It has too often lacked the institutions that make regulations meaningful. Perhaps that is why the commercial bus feels less like public transport than a moving census of deferred dreams. Every morning it gathers strangers whose lives would never otherwise intersect and reminds us that the country’s greatest common language is not ethnicity, religion or politics, but quiet perseverance. The accountant, the trader, the mechanic, the graduate and the widow may vote differently and pray differently, but they all understand the arithmetic of survival. That is also why the preacher is not really the central figure in this story. The tomato seller is. She never interrupted the sermon because survival had already become her liturgy. She needed no microphone to testify. Her gospel was written in prices that rose faster than her earnings, in children whose appetites ignored inflation, and in the fragile hope that tomorrow’s market might be kinder than today’s. When the bus finally reached her stop, she lifted her bags with the same care she had shown when she boarded, stepped into the morning and disappeared into the crowd. The preacher’s words remained inside the bus. Her work continued outside it. Perhaps that is where every public policy should ultimately be judged. Not by the applause it attracts, the headlines it generates or the impression of decisiveness it creates, but by a far simpler question. When the woman carrying the tomatoes gets off the bus, is her journey towards dignity any shorter than it was before? If the answer is no, then we may have regulated another symptom while leaving the disease untouched. Everything else is conversation. She still has tomatoes to sell. The post Salvation in the bus!, by Stephanie Shaakaa appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 2027 Presidency: Rivers people will decide who wins — Reuben Abati; Rufai Oseni disagrees
items.description: * No, Wike will actualise his boast, will deliver Tinubu – Rufai Oseni By Juliet Umeh The political temperature ahead of the 2027 general election rose another notch this week as comments by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, that Rivers State was already secured for President Bola Tinubu triggered a heated debate on ARISE Television’s The Morning Show. Read Also: Tinubu’s EFCC directive over Osun govt’s account sparks fresh questions over agency’s independence The programme also examined claims by Catholic leaders that the Presidency should pay closer attention to the realities facing Nigerians, with the show’s anchors disagreeing over whether President Tinubu is being shielded from public opinion. The controversy followed Wike’s declaration during his media chat in Abuja that politicians eyeing Rivers State for the 2027 presidential election should “forget it,” insisting that the state belongs politically to President Tinubu. “I am telling you, let nobody make a mistake. The only person that can win Rivers State is Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu,” the minister declared, describing himself as “a political realist.” The remarks immediately generated reactions on social media, with many users arguing that such comments could discourage voters and undermine confidence in the electoral process. On ARISE Television, Ayo Mairo-Ese urged Nigerians not to interpret Wike’s comments as a foregone conclusion, describing them as political posturing intended to unsettle opponents. “What he was doing is what we call mind games. It is ‘political big speak’. It is psychological warfare,” she said. According to her, regardless of political influence, elections are ultimately decided by voters. “Wike has one vote, just like every other Nigerian. The people of Rivers State will determine who emerges as the winner.” She, however, warned that influential political figures should exercise caution because statements suggesting that election outcomes have already been determined could deepen voter apathy. She also challenged the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, to strengthen public confidence by conducting elections that leave no room for manipulation. “INEC has to demonstrate that every vote counts and that elections are free, fair and credible,” she added. But co-anchor Rufai Oseni disagreed sharply with Mairo-Ese’s interpretation, arguing that Wike’s remarks should not be dismissed as mere political posturing because they reflected what many Nigerians already perceive about the country’s electoral system. Oseni argued that the minister’s confidence was rooted in his political influence and controversies surrounding the 2023 presidential election in Rivers State where figues declared didn’t tally with the ones on IREV which he said the BBC pointed out in a special report on Ngeria. Although he said that Wike’s statements reinforced public distrust in democracy, he was ready to bet with anybody that Wike’a claims would come to pass. “With due respect, he is not saying what he has not done. He is saying what he has done,” Oseni said, citing reports that questioned aspects of the 2023 election in Rivers and recalling Wike’s own claims about his dominance of the state’s political structure. He argued that pretending such fears do not exist would only deepen public cynicism, insisting that many Nigerians already doubt whether elections truly reflect the will of the people. “We keep saying we don’t want voter apathy, but many people already believe the process is a charade already,” he said. He maintained that many Nigerians already believe the electoral process is compromised and that journalists should confront that perception rather than dismiss it in the name of encouraging voter participation. Dr. Reuben Abati, however, rejected Rufai’s position, insisting that no politician has the constitutional authority to determine electoral outcomes. “Wike is just like every other Nigerian qualified to vote. He has only one vote,” Abati said. “He cannot sit today and announce the outcome of the 2027 election in Rivers State.” Describing Wike’s position as “a trip of delusion,” Abati stressed that only INEC is empowered by law to declare election results. He urged Rivers voters not to surrender their democratic rights because of political pronouncements. “The people of Rivers State have the right to go out and make their own informed choice,” he said, adding that those who attempt to undermine the electoral process should be held accountable. The discussion later shifted to criticism of the Tinubu administration by Catholic leaders following recent comments by Archbishop Emeritus Cardinal John Onaiyekan and Monsignor Obiora Ike. While some commentators suggested that those around the President were shielding him from the realities confronting Nigerians, Rufai disagreed. “There is no way the President will not know about all these things. He knows,” he said. According to him, President Tinubu has repeatedly responded to public criticism during meetings with religious leaders and traditional rulers, showing that he is fully aware of the hardship facing citizens. “The issue is not awareness. The issue is whether the government’s narrative is landing with Nigerians,” he argued. He noted that although the administration continues to defend its economic reforms, many Nigerians remain unconvinced because of rising hardship, insecurity and the high cost of living. Abati took a different view, defending the right of religious leaders to speak on national issues. He said the Catholic Church has historically challenged governments whenever it considered it necessary in the public interest. “The Catholic Church has a reputation for speaking its mind. They are not in the business of opposing the government for the sake of it,” he said. He added that the government should see such interventions as constructive criticism rather than hostility. “What we want in Nigeria is a prophetic Church that defends the interest of the people and speaks truth to power.” The exchanges reflected growing national anxiety over electoral credibility, governance and public trust ahead of the 2027 general election, with the three analysts offering sharply different interpretations of whether Wike’s declaration was merely political bravado or a reflection of deeper concerns about Nigeria’s democratic process. items.title: Muslim Muslim Ticket: Christians, Get Out?, by Stephanie Shaakaa
items.description: Every nation is built twice. The first construction is the one we can see. Roads are laid, airports are commissioned, constitutions are written, courts are established, and governments come and go. This is the architecture of the state, the visible framework through which power is exercised and public life is organized. Read Also: 25 children from Kebbi, Kwara, Niger died in terrorists’ captivity — Lawmaker The second construction is less tangible but infinitely more important. It takes place in the minds of citizens. It is built from trust, recognition, and the quiet conviction that despite differences of ethnicity, religion, language, and region, the country belongs equally to all who call it home. A nation survives not because it possesses institutions but because enough people believe those institutions belong to them. That belief is easy to overlook when it is healthy. Like the foundations beneath a building, it attracts little attention precisely because it is doing its job. Citizens go about their lives, elections are held, governments change, and the republic appears secure. Yet history repeatedly shows that the emotional foundations of a country can weaken long before any visible cracks appear in the structure above them. It is against this backdrop that the decision by the All Progressives Congress to retain President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and Vice President Kashim Shettima on a second consecutive Muslim Muslim ticket has generated a reaction that extends far beyond routine political disagreement. To many of its defenders, the controversy appears difficult to understand. They see a political party making a calculation about how best to retain power. They see incumbency, electoral arithmetic, regional alignments, and the practical realities of democratic competition. What many of them fail to appreciate is that political decisions are rarely interpreted solely through the intentions of those who make them. They are interpreted through the experiences of those who receive them. Politics is not merely a struggle over power. It is also a language through which societies communicate recognition, belonging, and status. Every appointment, alliance, nomination, and electoral ticket sends a signal about who is visible within the national imagination and who is expected to accept a more peripheral role. Human beings do not simply want to be governed competently. They want to know that they count. The Constitution, of course, does not require religious balancing. A political party is free to nominate candidates of its choosing, and supporters of the present arrangement argue that competence and electability should matter more than identity. There is merit in the desire to move beyond religious considerations in public life. The difficulty is that Nigeria is not a society in which questions of identity can be wished away by declaration. It is a federation of extraordinary diversity whose stability has long depended on a mixture of formal safeguards and informal understandings designed to reassure competing communities that the republic belongs to all of them. The federal character principle did not emerge by accident. Neither did the unwritten habits of regional and religious balancing that have shaped political life for decades. These arrangements were not necessarily perfect, but they reflected a recognition that in a country as plural as Nigeria, inclusion is not a sentimental aspiration. It is part of the mechanism through which trust is maintained. People rarely admire the beams that hold up a roof. They notice them only when somebody begins to remove them. The anxiety surrounding the current ticket becomes easier to understand when viewed within a broader historical context. For eight years under Muhammadu Buhari, many Nigerians observed a concentration of political authority in the hands of Muslim officeholders. A Muslim President and a Muslim Vice President governed alongside a Muslim Senate President, a Muslim Deputy Senate President, a Muslim Speaker of the House of Representatives, and a Muslim Deputy Speaker. Each office may have emerged through its own political process, yet citizens do not experience power as a series of isolated appointments. They experience it as a pattern. Politics is interpreted cumulatively, and cumulative patterns acquire symbolic meaning regardless of the intentions behind them. This helps explain why comparisons with the Abiola Kingibe ticket of 1993 often generate more heat than understanding. The comparison is superficially appealing because both men were Muslims. Yet politics is not experienced through demographics alone. It is experienced through context. Nigerians certainly knew the religious identities of Moshood Abiola and Babagana Kingibe, but religion did not occupy the same place in the political imagination that it does today. The election was widely understood as part of a larger democratic struggle against military rule. Citizens argued about democracy, transition, governance, and national renewal. The ticket was not generally interpreted as a statement about religious representation because the political atmosphere of the period was not saturated with the same anxieties that shape contemporary debates. A precedent stripped of its context ceases to function as a precedent. It becomes little more than a convenient slogan. The significance of the present controversy therefore lies not simply in the composition of a ticket but in the evolution of what that composition represents. The first Muslim Muslim ticket was defended as an exceptional arrangement justified by exceptional political circumstances. Whether one accepted that explanation or not, it was presented as a departure from convention rather than a replacement for it. The second ticket changes the conversation. It asks Nigerians to treat the exception as normal. It transforms what was once defended as a temporary necessity into something that increasingly resembles a principle. That distinction is at the heart of the current debate because exceptions reassure citizens that a broader norm still exists, whereas normalization inevitably raises questions about whether the norm exists at all. These concerns have been intensified by the broader condition of the country. Across Nigeria, citizens are united by burdens that care little about religious identity. Inflation does not distinguish between churchgoers and worshippers at the mosque. Rising food prices, insecurity, unemployment, and economic uncertainty are experienced across communities. The trader in Kano, the farmer in Benue, the teacher in Enugu, the mechanic in Kaduna, and the civil servant in Lagos all inhabit the same landscape of anxiety and diminishing certainty. Shared suffering has become one of the few truly national experiences in contemporary Nigeria. Yet it is precisely during periods of hardship that questions of representation acquire greater rather than lesser significance. Citizens are often willing to overlook symbolic grievances when governments deliver prosperity, security, and confidence in the future. They become less willing to do so when public trust is already under strain. Under such circumstances, concerns about inclusion cease to be abstract debates about identity. They become intertwined with deeper questions about fairness, legitimacy, and whether the sacrifices demanded by national life are being matched by an equal sense of belonging. This is where the argument over the Muslim Muslim ticket ultimately transcends religion. At its core lies a question about the nature of the Nigerian republic itself. Is inclusion a principle that remains central to nation building, or has it become a convenience that can be set aside whenever political circumstances make it expedient to do so? Can a federation as diverse as Nigeria afford to become casual about the symbolic reassurances that have helped sustain it, or does doing so risk weakening the very trust upon which national cohesion depends? History offers no simple answers, but it does provide a warning. Nations rarely come apart because one group wins an election. They rarely collapse because another group loses. The more dangerous process is usually quieter and more gradual. It begins when enough citizens start to feel that they are becoming spectators in a country they helped build. It gathers strength when political competition is increasingly interpreted through the language of exclusion rather than participation. It matures when communities that once regarded themselves as stakeholders begin to wonder whether they are merely being asked to endorse decisions made without them in mind. Countries seldom recognize this process while it is unfolding. Their institutions continue to function. Elections are held. Courts remain open. Economic activity goes on. To the casual observer, everything appears normal. What changes is something less visible and therefore easier to ignore. Citizens begin to lose confidence that the nation sees them in the same way they once believed it did. They continue to obey its laws, pay its taxes, and participate in its politics, yet the sense of shared ownership that binds a diverse population together begins to weaken. The phrase “Christians, get out” is not the literal message of a second Muslim Muslim ticket. No one is being expelled from the republic. No law is being enacted to deny anyone citizenship or participation in public life. The danger is subtler than that. It lies in the possibility that millions of citizens may gradually conclude that visibility within the highest symbols of national life has become negotiable while their obligations to the nation remain permanent. Every republic eventually faces moments that reveal how it understands itself. Such moments are rarely dramatic. More often they emerge through decisions that appear practical, defensible, and politically advantageous at the time. Years later, however, those same decisions are remembered not for the calculations that produced them but for what they revealed about the relationship between power and belonging. The question before Nigeria is therefore larger than the composition of a single electoral ticket. It is whether the federation still believes that every major community should be able to look at the highest symbols of national life and recognize itself there. Because once large numbers of citizens cease to feel reflected in the republic, they do not stop being citizens. They simply stop feeling that the republic belongs to them in quite the same way. And history suggests that by the time a nation notices that loss, the damage is usually much further advanced than it appears. The post Muslim Muslim Ticket: Christians, Get Out?, by Stephanie Shaakaa appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Trump et l’Iran | L’échec d’une diplomatie du bluff
items.description: Cinq mois après le lancement de l’opération Epic Fury, la stratégie américaine conduite par Donald Trump et ses conseillers de «pression maximale» contre l’Iran s’est muée en impasse politique et militaire. Entre la réticence des alliés du Golfe, l’épuisement des stocks de missiles et l’approche des élections de mi-mandat, Donald Trump se retrouve pris au piège de sa propre diplomatie du bluff. Dr Abderrahmane Cherfouh * Lorsque les premiers missiles américains et israéliens ont frappé le sol iranien fin février dans le cadre de l’opération Epic Fury , Donald Trump reprenait une rhétorique qu’il affectionne : celle de la «paix par la force» théâtralisée. Sur ses réseaux sociaux, le président américain promettait au peuple iranien une «libération imminente» , affirmant que le moment était venu de se libérer une fois pour toutes du joug des ayatollahs. Les analystes les plus avertis s’interrogeaient sur la viabilité d’une telle posture : s’agissait-il d’une réelle démonstration de puissance ou des prémices d’un aveuglement stratégique ? Cinq mois plus tard, la réponse ne fait plus de doute. Le calcul trumpien reposait sur une équation simpliste issue du monde des affaires : appliquer une pression maximale par un déluge de feu pour provoquer l’effondrement immédiat du régime ou forcer une capitulation sans condition. Mais la géopolitique des crises de haute intensité ne répond pas aux règles de la négociation immobilière. La résilience de Téhéran face à l’impuissance de la surenchère Au lieu de provoquer le soulèvement populaire escompté ou la panique au sommet de l’État théocratique, l’attaque a déclenché un réflexe de survie institutionnel à Téhéran. La République islamique a promptement verrouillé l’appareil sécuritaire intérieur, étouffant toute contestation naissante, tout en déployant une stratégie de riposte asymétrique et régionale. Face aux ultimatums répétés de Washington promettant «une destruction encore jamais vue dans l’histoire» , Téhéran a choisi la fermeté et le harcèlement à distance. L’incapacité de Donald Trump à faire plier le régime est devenue flagrante : la surenchère verbale, dépourvue de stratégie terrestre ou de vision politique à long terme, a fini par étaler les limites du pouvoir militaire américain. L’évolution du conflit au cours des cinq derniers mois a mis à nu la méthode Trump : une alternance permanente entre menaces apocalyptiques, reculades précipitées et décisions impulsives dictées par l’humeur du moment plutôt que par une doctrine cohérente. La régionalisation du conflit (mars-avril) : Téhéran réplique en ciblant les infrastructures stratégiques et les bases alliées à travers le Moyen-Orient, étendant l’instabilité bien au-delà des frontières iraniennes. Illusion du «deal» et le répit éphémère (mai-juin) : Pris de court par l’enlisement et obsédé par les indicateurs économiques, Trump décrète unilatéralement un cessez-le-feu en proclamant prématurément «victoire» . Sans accord politique de fond, cette trêve n’a été qu’un mirage. Crise navale et suspension des frappes (juillet-août) : la reprise des tensions dans le détroit d’Ormuz pousse la Maison-Blanche à ordonner de nouvelles frappes, avant de devoir se résoudre à les suspendre face à l’absence de résultats probants. L’Iran a tenu | La fin de l’ère américaine Le tournant saoudien et la fracture des alliés du Golfe L’élément déclencheur du récent changement de cap à Washington ne provient pas d’une prise de conscience interne, mais d’un rappel à la réalité venu du Golfe. Subissant de plein fouet les tirs de missiles et de drones iraniens sur leurs raffineries, leurs ports et leurs aéroports, les monarchies arabes ont exprimé un ras-le-bol stratégique. Le point de rupture a été atteint lors d’un entretien téléphonique entre Mohammed Ben Salmane et Donald Trump. Le souverain saoudien a demandé sans détour au président américain de cesser immédiatement les bombardements sur l’Iran. Le constat présenté par Riyad était sans appel : faute de succès militaire décisif et sans perspective réelle de changement de régime, poursuivre ces frappes ne faisait que transformer les pays du Golfe en cibles privilégiées, tout en resserrant les rangs de la population iranienne derrière ses dirigeants. En Europe, la gestion de la crise par Donald Trump a fini de détruire le peu de confiance qui subsistait envers le parapluie diplomatique américain. Dès le lancement d’ Epic Fury , les chancelleries européennes (Paris, Berlin, Londres) avaient mis en garde contre les risques d’une escalade incontrôlée. Aujourd’hui, l’exaspération des dirigeants européens est totale. Face aux revirements incessants de la Maison-Blanche — qui passe en quelques jours de la menace de guerre totale à des appels du pied pour négocier —, l’Europe déplore l’absence complète de concertation et l’aventurisme d’une administration incapable de fixer un cap stratégique clair. La diplomatie européenne se retrouve contrainte de gérer les répercussions sécuritaires et migratoires d’un conflit qu’elle n’a pas voulu et qu’elle ne peut pas enrayer seule. Limites techniques et asphyxie économique Sur le plan interne comme international, le coût de cette diplomatie du bluff est devenu insupportable. Sur le terrain militaire comme sur le plan politique domestique, Washington se heurte à des contraintes matérielles et électorales majeures. Comme l’a analysé Sébastien Boussois, chercheur spécialiste du monde arabe et directeur de l’Institut géopolitique européen, la marge de manœuvre du président américain s’est considérablement réduite : «Donald Trump ne veut pas forcément frapper, n’en a pas forcément les moyens. Il y avait un problème de missiles, puis il avait un problème d’intercepteurs. Et puis, il y a aussi une opinion qui, à l’approche des élections de mi-mandat, risque de commencer à se détourner du président américain» . Ce double verrou — l’épuisement des stocks d’armement de haute précision et la crainte d’un désaveu dans les urnes — paralyse l’action américaine. Parallèlement, en perturbant gravement le trafic maritime dans le détroit d’Ormuz — canal vital par lequel transite un cinquième du pétrole mondial —, le conflit a provoqué une flambée spectaculaire des cours du baril. Les consommateurs du monde entier paient aujourd’hui au prix fort à la pompe les hésitations de Washington, alimentant une inflation globale qui menace de faire basculer plusieurs économies dans la récession. Cinq mois après le lancement de l’opération Epic Fury , le bilan de Donald Trump est celui d’une impasse stratégique majeure. En pensant que des coups de bluff répétés, des ultimatums sur les réseaux sociaux et des sautes d’humeur diplomatiques tiendraient lieu de politique étrangère, le président américain a étalé les limites de son leadership. Désormais contraint par le roi d’Arabie saoudite à suspendre ses frappes, contesté par son opinion publique, désavoué par ses alliés européens et sous la pression d’une crise économique mondiale qu’il a lui-même contribué à alimenter, Trump offre le spectacle d’une puissance paralysée. Les ultimatums non suivis d’effets ont créé l’accoutumance chez l’adversaire et la méfiance chez les alliés. L’étalage de force brute aura, in fine , mis à nu l’incapacité d’un homme à prendre les décisions justes face au temps long et complexe de la géopolitique. * Médecin algérien basé au Canada. Les menaces de Trump ne font plus peur à personne ! L’article Trump et l’Iran | L’échec d’une diplomatie du bluff est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Govt restores original medical board for exhumation of Mir Raza’s body
items.description: • Corpse of IBA graduate to be dug up for fresh autopsy today • Exhumation planned for Friday postponed after family objected to abrupt reconstitution of board KARACHI: After a day of uncertainty over the exhumation of the body of IBA graduate and businessman Mir Raza Ali, the Sindh government on Friday evening restored the original medical board, which is set to exhume the body on Saturday (today). The exhumation, which was scheduled for Friday morning, was postponed after Raza’s family objected to the abrupt reconstitution of a medical board and inclusion of members from outside Karachi division. Raza’s body was found in bushes in Gulistan-i-Jauhar last month, a day after he went missing on July 28. On Thursday, a judicial magistrate had allowed the exhumation of the body on an application filed by Raza’s father, Mir Hussain Ali, directing the police surgeon and the Sindh health secretary to constitute a medical board for the exhumation. The Sindh health department then constituted an eight-member board, with Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed as the convener. Prof Dr Naseem Ahmed of Dow University of Health Sciences, Dr Farah Waseem of Jinnah Sindh Medical University, Amir Hassan Khan of Citizens Police Liaison Committee, Additional Police Surgeon Dr Sirichand, Dr Kamran Khan and Dr Daniyal Mirza of Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre and Dr Mohammed Yaseen, the admin in-charge of the police surgeon office, were the other members of the board. However, in the small hours of Friday morning, the board was reconstituted through an order issued by the director general of the Sindh health department. While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new five-member board, its members were changed to Prof Dr Zakiuddin from DUHS, Prof Dr Kazi Akbar and Prof Dr Abid Hussain Chang from Liaquat University of Medical and Health Sciences and Hyderabad Police Surgeon Dr Waseem Khan. On Friday morning, Raza’s family was present at the Tariq Road graveyard for the exhumation. But, the exhumation was deferred, with the counsel for Raza’s family, Jibran Nasir, telling the media that they had informed the investigating officer that the family had rejected the reconstituted board and would not accept an exhumation by it “under any circumstances”. Standing alongside Raza’s father, Advocate Nasir accused the authorities of trying to bury the facts and held the police, health department and the Sindh government responsible for the delay. The family could not allow the exhumation to be performed by members whose “qualifications and intentions were under question”, he added. He recalled that the previous night, DG-health dismissed the original board and reconstituted it, adding four names from Hyderabad. He claimed that following outcry over the reconstituted board, the DG-health then issued a “backdated notification at around 10am on Friday, stating that more members may be added, but the four chosen by him should also remain a part of it”. He added that they still had not been informed why the original board was reconstituted. The lawyer said they would not be making any demands to the police. Raza’s father was now directly raising questions to Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah and PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, he said. He asserted that they only trusted the original eight-member board, adding, “Sindh government, they were hired by you. And if they are not competent enough, then how were they appointed in the first place?” Advocate Nasir also submitted a letter to the police surgeon on Friday, wherein he formally informed her of the family’s non-consent and stated that the reconstituted board was in “complete violation and negation” of the court’s order and had no legal basis. He held that it carried no binding value and was nothing “but a malicious attempt to interfere with judicial proceedings initiated by the court” and any directive in support of the board shall be viewed as a “further malicious attempt to provide cover to an illegal act and sabotage fair and transparent investigation”. He said the family had not consented to the exhumation by the reconstituted board and warned that any attempt to proceed with the exhumation under the reconstituted medical board will be a violation of the dignity of the deceased, will put evidence at risk and will be a “blatant” contempt of court. Late in the evening, the Sindh health secretary issued a notification, restoring the original eight-member medical board. Following the notification, the police surgeon sent a letter to the magistrate concerned and other members of the board, informing them that the exhumation is scheduled to be conducted at the graveyard adjacent to Rehmania Masjid at 11am on Saturday (today). Prior to the restoration of the original medical board, the police surgeon expressed her frustration over “impediments” in a post on X. The post was deleted after the government restored the eight-member board. It may be noted that the case took a new turn when the police surgeon told a private news channel on Tuesday that the post-mortem findings had raised several questions, as some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs. Her interview prompted the police authorities to issue a statement, terming such observations as having the potential to adversely affect the ongoing investigation. Published in Dawn, August 8th, 2026

items.title: 38 morts en une semaine : les failles du transport par bus en Algérie
items.description: Les accidents de bus ont fait 38 morts et plus de 100 blessés en moins d’une semaine en Algérie (du 31 juillet au 6 août). Dans cet entretien, l’économiste Brahim Guendouzi analyse à TSA l’état du secteur du transport par bus en Algérie, pointe ses failles et les principaux facteurs à l’origine des accidents d’autocars. Les accidents de bus font beaucoup de morts en Algérie. En moins d’une semaine, du 31 juillet au 6 août derniers, 38 personnes ont perdu la vie dans des accidents d’autocars. Dans ce contexte, pourquoi l'État ne reprend-il pas la main sur le transport routier en commun en relançant des entreprises comme la SNTV ? Brahim Guendouzi : L’ouverture sur l’investissement privé et l’adoption de la loi sur la concurrence ont fait que de nombreux secteurs d’activité, dont le transport routier, sont devenus ouverts et concurrentiels. Pour assurer une meilleure mobilité des personnes et des marchandises, des lignes de transport sont accordées à l’intérieur des wilayas et entre wilayas. L’action de l’État y est toutefois présente à travers la gestion des gares routières, la tarification, les autorisations administratives délivrées sur telle ou telle ligne, etc. Il faut rappeler que l’expérience des transports de voyageurs assurés par la SNTV n’était pas aussi efficace du fait même de la faiblesse de la flotte de bus pour assurer et couvrir l’ensemble des destinations à travers toutes les wilayas du pays. Des voyageurs subissaient des désagréments en termes de délais d’attente, de reports ou carrément d’absence de ligne et donc il fallait faire des détours pour arriver à la destination souhaitée. L’investissement privé a pu donner plus de flexibilité au transport des voyageurs et a facilité la mobilité des personnes et des familles. Dans de nombreux pays du monde, le transport par bus est du ressort de l'État via des entreprises ou des régies publiques. Pourquoi l'Algérie ne fera-t-elle pas de même ? Brahim Guendouzi : L’État a préféré se désengager du transport routier de voyageurs, qu’il a laissé au secteur privé, pour se consacrer plus au développement du transport par le rail, car nécessitant de gros investissements (train, tramway et métro), et ce, du fait même du concept de monopole naturel. Néanmoins, s’agissant des grandes villes, à l’exemple de la capitale, le transport urbain est assuré par une régie publique comme l’ETUSA. Avec la multiplication des accidents de la route impliquant des bus, le privé a-t-il montré son échec dans le domaine du transport ? Brahim Guendouzi : Il faut reconnaître que le secteur privé dans sa globalité a su hisser le transport routier à un niveau appréciable en termes de nombre de dessertes assurées, des conditions de transport et des délais, sachant que la tarification est imposée par l’État. Ce n’est pas parce qu’il y a des accidents de la route qu’il faut directement blâmer les transporteurs routiers dans leur ensemble. Il y a certes des responsabilités à assumer dans chaque cas d’accident, mais il ne faut pas faire porter le chapeau à tous les transporteurs. Un diagnostic reste à faire pour pouvoir évaluer le secteur du transport des voyageurs et dresser un plan de développement en associant plusieurs parties prenantes afin de pouvoir résorber les contraintes constatées. D’ores et déjà, il existe des failles auxquelles il faudra apporter des solutions, comme par exemple l’état des routes, le défaut de signalisation, l’absence de maintenance des véhicules, la saturation sur un certain nombre de routes, la façon de conduire souvent dangereuse d’un grand nombre de chauffeurs, aussi bien des poids lourds que des légers (excès de vitesse, non-respect des distances de sécurité, manœuvres risquées, …) portant atteinte à la sécurité routière. L’atomisation du transport par bus avec de petits transporteurs qui courent derrière le bénéfice est-elle la cause de la détérioration de ce secteur vital ? Brahim Guendouzi : Le transport routier de voyageurs est fortement atomisé et très concurrentiel. Dès lors que la tarification est imposée par l’État et que par ailleurs le prix du gasoil est subventionné, la rentabilité du transporteur se joue au niveau de deux éléments : les frais de personnel, dont les chauffeurs, et les coûts de la maintenance, qui peuvent être élevés en raison de l’état vétuste des bus. S’agissant du recrutement des chauffeurs, les plus expérimentés et bien formés sont évidemment recherchés, mais avec des salaires conséquents. Certains transporteurs, ne pouvant pas assurer des niveaux de salaires élevés à des chauffeurs, se rabattent sur les moins expérimentés. Il en est de même de la maintenance qui pourrait être négligée du fait des délais d’immobilisation des véhicules et des frais élevés à engager. En définitive, la forte concurrence dans le transport routier fait que certains transporteurs n’arrivent pas à assurer une rentabilité de leurs activités et donc se retrouvent fragilisés en termes de qualité de recrutement des chauffeurs et de la maîtrise de la maintenance d’un parc roulant vieillissant. Aussi, il y a lieu de renforcer le contrôle à ce niveau, car toute négligence serait fatale. D’ailleurs, la plupart des accidents sont causés soit par une erreur humaine (façon de conduire des chauffeurs) soit par des défauts techniques de mécanique dans les bus. Vient ensuite l’état des routes. L’article 38 morts en une semaine : les failles du transport par bus en Algérie est apparu en premier sur TSA .
