items.title: Le secteur automobile allemand va mal
items.description: Face à la montée irrépressible des voitures chinoises et à la crise énergétique induite par le boycott européen du gaz bon marché russe, certains constructeurs automobiles allemands sont obligés de licencier une partie de leur personnel qui n’est pas lié à la production, d’autres vont jusqu’à licencier des ouvriers de production. Habib Glenza , à Lodz . L’effondrement de l’économie allemande a commencé après la décision de l’UE de boycotter le gaz russe, très bon marché. Cette décision lourde de conséquences rentre dans le cadre des sanctions européennes à l’encontre de la Russie. Les droits de douane imposés par Trump et la guerre au Moyen-Orient ont littéralement mis à genoux la première économie européenne, jadis prospère grâce à l’énergie russe bon marché. Entre-temps les voitures chinoises ont envahi le monde entier avec des prix qui défient toute concurrence. Pour réduire le coût de production, certains constructeurs allemands sont obligés de licencier une partie du personnel qui n’est pas lié à la production, d’autres vont jusqu’à licencier des ouvriers de production. Le constructeur BMW prévoit de supprimer 8 000 emplois d’ici fin 2027. C’est l’entreprise qui a annoncé son plan de licenciements qui commencera à être mis en œuvre à partir d’octobre 2026 et s’achèvera à la fin de l’année prochaine. Un plan de départs volontaires pour réduire les coûts de production Les personnes concernées par cette suppression sont tous les employés des usines du constructeur munichois en Allemagne qui n’occupent pas des postes directement liés à la production. Autrement dit, les victimes directes seront les employés de bureau. L’idée est d’offrir à près de la moitié de son personnel en Allemagne la possibilité d’adhérer à un plan de départs volontaires et ainsi d’atteindre l’objectif de 8 000 emplois en moins. Un plan de réduction des effectifs qui permettra à BMW de réaliser des économies substantielles, le constructeur estimant qu’il réduira ses coûts de personnel Actuellement, selon les données publiées par le Wall Street Journal , environ 84 000 des 154 000 employés de BMW travaillent en Allemagne. BMW rejoint ainsi la liste croissante des entreprises du secteur automobile, qui traverse en Allemagne l’une de ses pires périodes. Volkswagen, Porsche, Audi et Mercedes suppriment des emplois Le constructeur automobile munichois emboîte le pas à d’autres comme Volkswagen, Porsche, Audi et Mercedes, qui ont annoncé ces derniers mois des plans de réduction d’effectifs. Le principal facteur déclencheur de cette crise dans le secteur automobile allemand est le marché chinois, devenu l’un des principaux concurrents des entreprises allemandes. Les droits de douane imposés par les États-Unis et la crise au Moyen-Orient aggravent également les difficultés auxquelles est confronté le secteur, l’un des piliers historiques de l’économie allemande qui, ces derniers temps, subit des coups de plus en plus durs et s’effondre de plus en plus. Volkswagen perd un milliard d’euros en trois mois L’article Le secteur automobile allemand va mal est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: CUTS challenges DVLA over escalating ‘delinquency’ charges
items.description: The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA) is facing calls to suspend its escalating “delinquency” charges on expired driver’s licences until it publicly establishes the legal authority, approval process and formula used to determine the fees. The demand has come from CUTS International, a public policy think tank, which argues that the charges lack clear backing in the Road Traffic Regulations, 2012 (L.I. 2180) and could unfairly penalise motorists whose licences have expired even when they have not driven during the period. In a statement issued on August 9, 2026, the Director of the West Africa Regional Centre of CUTS International, Accra, Appiah Kusi Adomako, said the DVLA should disclose the precise statutory instrument and approved fee schedule authorising each charge. Under the DVLA’s Summary of Licensing and Other Activity Rates for 2026, renewing a licence before its expiry costs GH¢127. However, the amount increases to GH¢204.25 for a licence expired by between one day and six months, GH¢279.25 for seven to 12 months, GH¢315.25 for up to two years, GH¢352.25 for up to four years and GH¢404.25 for more than four years. CUTS said similar escalating charges applied to the replacement of expired licences. “The DVLA must show Ghanaians the law, the approved fee schedule and the formula behind every cedi it collects as a delinquency charge. Public power must rest on law. If the Authority cannot point to a clear legal basis for each charge, it must stop collecting the money and refund affected licence holders,” Mr Adomako said. Legal basis questioned At the centre of CUTS’ objection is Regulation 33 of L.I. 2180, which provides for the renewal of a driver’s licence both before and after its expiry. The organisation said the regulations expressly recognise that licences may be renewed after expiry and separately provide for an offence where a person fails to renew as prescribed. Under the law, a person who fails to renew a driver’s licence as prescribed is liable, upon summary conviction, to a fine of between 10 and 25 penalty units, imprisonment for up to 30 days, or both. CUTS argues that the distinction is important because the law provides for enforcement and prosecution where an offence is committed, rather than automatically treating every expired licence as evidence of unlawful driving. It is therefore asking the DVLA to clarify whether the escalating amounts are approved renewal fees, administrative penalties or another form of charge. “If the amounts are penalties, the DVLA must explain the legal process that permits an administrative system to impose them without proof of driving during the period of expiry, without a hearing and without a finding by a court,” the statement said. Mr Adomako stressed that CUTS was not advocating driving with an expired licence. “CUTS is not encouraging anyone to drive with an expired licence. Driving without a valid licence must attract lawful enforcement. Our concern is different: the DVLA should not presume that every person with an expired licence continued to drive, then impose an automatic escalating charge without first establishing the legal and factual basis,” he said. Expiry does not prove driving CUTS said the mere expiry of a licence should not automatically be equated with unlawful driving. It noted that a licence holder could be living abroad, studying, ill or simply not driving for an extended period. Such a person, it argued, could return years later and seek to renew the licence without having driven on Ghanaian roads during the period of expiry. Mr Adomako said such motorists should be encouraged to regularise their licences before returning to the road rather than being treated as though they had committed an offence. “That citizen should be encouraged to regularise his licence before returning to the road. He should not be branded delinquent and punished as though expiry itself proves unlawful driving. The system must distinguish an expired document from the separate act of driving without a valid licence,” he said. CUTS also questioned the use of the word “delinquency”, saying it could imply wrongdoing before the circumstances of an individual licence holder had been established. It proposed the use of neutral descriptions such as “renewal after expiry”, alongside clear criteria for waivers, exemptions or proof that a vehicle was not being used. Concern over GH¢181 data amendment fee The think tank also raised concerns about a GH¢181 charge for amending a licence holder’s electronic records. It argued that charging motorists to update basic information such as telephone numbers or residential addresses could discourage people from keeping their records current. According to CUTS, accurate contact and residential information is important for road safety, identity verification, criminal investigations and emergency communication. “The DVLA should design fees to support compliance, not discourage it. When a citizen wants to correct an address or telephone number, the Authority gains better data. Charging GH¢181 for a basic update risks leaving the database outdated and weakens the public interest the database is meant to serve,” Mr Adomako said. CUTS has consequently called on Parliament to conduct an urgent inquiry into the legality, approval and administration of the DVLA’s escalating “delinquency” charges. It also wants the DVLA and the Ghana Police Service to clarify their respective enforcement responsibilities so the public can clearly understand the processes for investigating, prosecuting and sanctioning drivers who operate vehicles without valid licences.

items.title: Child among three killed in Russian missile attacks near Kyiv
items.description: At least three people, including a child, have been killed in overnight Russian attacks near the Ukrainian capital Kyiv. In the early hours of Saturday missiles hit east of the capital and witnesses reported hearing powerful explosions just days after strikes across Ukraine killed 21 people. Falling debris damaged apartment buildings and cars, while a fire broke out at a separate building, the head of the regional military administration Timur Tkachenko said. He added that three others had been wounded in the ballistic missile strikes. Emergency crews were also fighting fires at a building and fuel tank in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaly Klitchko wrote on Telegram. Ukraine’s state emergency service DSNS shared photos showing garages, a business and a building on fire in Kyiv, adding: “The number of victims is being clarified.” President Volodymyr Zelensky has arrived in the Serbian capital Belgrade for his first visit after raising concerns about Ukraine’s capacity to fend off Russian missile attacks due to depleting interceptor stockpiles. Zelensky is is trying to build wider support for Ukraine, but Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić has refused to apply sanctions to Russia. Serbia is trying to join the EU and has provided aid to Ukraine and promised to help it rebuild after the war. The two leaders were set to discuss economic ties, relations with the EU and security issues in Belgrade. Earlier in the week, Zelensky said delays in receiving anti-ballistic systems from partners leads to “horrific casualties and destruction”, saying that having a stronger interceptor capability “could have saved lives” in recent deadly assaults. The president later said the supply of interceptors from allies had been “significantly reduced” this year. It came after Ukraine hit two oil refineries deep inside Russia along with Moscow-linked vessels in the Black Sea, which Zelensky said was intended to limit oil revenues used by Russia to “finance” its war in Ukraine. Recent mediation talks have faltered, leading to an escalation of attacks between both sides.

items.title: Delayed construction projects pollute air, put lives at risk
items.description: Life for residents and workers along the Adentan–Dodowa road was upended in 2024. A routine upgrade scheduled to take three years has left the community covered in dust and harmful pollutants, putting thousands of lives at risk. The project stalled early on, and experts say the failure to pay the contractor on time has led to delays that may mean this misery continues for the community even longer. The project is just one of many roadworks under the government’s “Big Push” infrastructure development programme across the country that are taking longer than promised. Delays, often caused by missed government payments to contractors, are leaving millions of Ghanaians exposed to increased risks of diseases linked to air pollution, such as asthma, heart disease, cancer and diabetes. “Here in Ghana, we don’t implement engineering projects well, especially government of Ghana-funded projects,” said Joseph Odei, a fellow of the Ghana Institution of Engineers. He said poor oversight and corruption are among the reasons projects are delayed. “They delay paying contractors, so they face challenges and vacate the project.” The 22-kilometre Adentan–Dodowa dual carriageway stretches from the Adentan Barrier through Katamanso, Oyibi and Gbortsui to the Dodowa Hospital Junction. The project is expected to ease traffic congestion between the Greater Accra, Eastern and Volta regions while improving road safety and reducing travel time. Experts agree it would boost economic activity in the region. The contract was awarded in March 2024 to the Ghanaian company Oswal Investments under a 36-month agreement. Inspecting the project a year later, Kwame Agbodza, Minister for Roads and Highways, conceded that the project had stalled, blaming the previous government’s failure to make agreed payments. Mr Agbodza said the Mahama government had settled the outstanding payments. Gabriel Foli, project manager for Oswal Investments, declined to comment for this story, but in July he told Channel One TV that delays were caused by property acquisition, negotiations over compensation for owners and the relocation of utility lines. He assured the public that the project was two-thirds complete and on track to be finished by March 2027. For residents, the roadworks are taking a heavy toll. People here are well aware of the dangers. Mary Adjiele, 50, says three of her grandchildren have developed severe coughs accompanied by high fevers since the work began. The family has been forced to spend much of its income on medical treatment at Alpha and Omega Hospital in Dodowa. “Cough with blood,” Adjiele said in Twi. “It is small streaks or drops of bright red blood that come with mucus from three of my grandchildren. The money we use for our business and family upkeep is now going into hospital bills.” Health experts warn that prolonged exposure to dust particles is dangerous. Fine particulate matter can enter the bloodstream, increasing the risk of chronic illnesses, including kidney and heart diseases, diabetes and cancer. “Road dust often has fine particles, cement, silica and vehicle exhaust,” said Dorcas Effah Agyeiwaa, a public health nurse at the community’s Amamorley Clinic. “When we breathe it in, it can irritate our airways and make asthma worse. That irritation can cause the blood vessels in the airways to break and lead to blood in the cough.” Health authorities say infrastructure development in Ghana is necessary to boost economic activity, but the health impacts cannot be ignored. They say communities across the country should not be left to deal with the health consequences of delays caused by government failures. The Ghana Health Service reports increasing cases of respiratory illnesses across the Greater Accra Region. According to Dr Robert Amesiya, Greater Accra Regional Director of Health Services, in the two years to 2023, hypertension – a disease closely linked to air pollution – was the fifth-highest cause of death in Accra, claiming 200 lives, while nearly 40,000 cases were reported. Asthma and cardiac cases also increased. “We thank the government for building the roads for our safety,” said Dr Amesiya in Twi. “But the dust on the construction roads is too much.” A spare-parts dealer operating along the road says the thick dust has made every working day a health challenge. Concerned about his wife’s worsening asthma and persistent coughing, he has asked her to stop assisting him at the shop. “We sell car parts, but the dust has filled my wife’s and my nose,” the dealer said in Twi. “I clean my shop every 20 minutes, but the dust keeps coming back. My wife has been coughing continuously. We have nowhere else to go because this business is our livelihood. We humbly appeal to the government to asphalt the road to reduce the dust. Our health matters too.” Provision shop owner Serwaa Ansah Opoku says the dust has left her battling constant illness. “Because of the dust on the road, when we wear our clothes, it turns brown,” she said in Twi. “We keep getting headaches. We take local herbal medicine and the drugs our doctors prescribed for us to take care of the headaches and blood pressure.” While waakye vendor Hamdia Ishmahill, a student, reports frequent coughs that have affected her business. “It worries me. The dust has reduced our customers who buy waakye from us,” the student said in Twi. “My mum is not able to come to the wayside to sell. I’m a student, so I normally come to support her. I always get coughs. But because people complain there is no food around, I’m forced to sell in the dust.” Traditional leaders are equally worried. Chief Adjie Kwashie, Linguist of Adenta Frafraha, said asthma cases within the community are increasing, with many residents complaining of worsening respiratory conditions. The traditional palace has been suspended because of the unhealthy environment. “We have elderly people who come to our palace reporting cases of asthma,” said Chief Kwashie in Twi. “We’ve asked them to tell the contractor to continue watering the road to reduce the dust. We’ve also reached out to the workers constructing the road. Once in a while, they come to sprinkle water on the road. We need asphalt on our road.” During his April 2026 visit, the Minister directed the contractor to regularly sprinkle water on the road to minimise dust and reduce its impact on surrounding communities, stressing that protecting residents’ health remains the responsibility of the contractor. “We expect a lot more speed,” Minister Agbodza said in Twi, speaking with engineers and the contractor. “This is another very important corridor which, when completed, will help significantly. So pay attention to it. While you are doing it, the dust will be to the minimum. We know it is difficult. We know it’s not easy to water continuously, but that is your responsibility, so don’t run away from it.” Ella Christine Esinam Nongo, Municipal Chief Executive for Adentan, has assured residents that the Assembly and the contractor are working together to reduce dust pollution. “Residents, please be a little patient with us,” an Assembly official said in Twi. “If the contractors come to fix it and there are still potholes, the same people will not be happy with us. We beg you. Since we have endured bad roads for a long time, give us a little time to fix it. Anytime the contractor is not around, the Assembly sprinkles water on the road.” Dr Amesiya urged residents to wear nose masks to minimise exposure to dust while efforts continue to control pollution along the construction corridor. This story is a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Clean Air Reporting project. Funding was provided by the Clean Air Fund, which had no say in the story’s content.

items.title: Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged ‘lover’
items.description: Gianni Infantino’s alleged lover was given a severance payment over the affair by Uefa while he was its general secretary, according to a Daily Telegraph investigation , external . A spokesman for the now Fifa president was reported to have told the paper Infantino “strongly denies these categorically untrue allegations”. Uefa, for whom Infantino was general secretary from 2009 to 2016, issued a statement confirming “a departure payment was made to the individual in question”. The allegations come as Infantino fights for his future as Fifa president following his aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors. BBC Sport has contacted Fifa and Infantino for comment. The Telegraph reported that Uefa paid a six-figure sum to the woman, who had an alleged relationship with Infantino, who is married, during his time at European football’s governing body. “Fifa president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue. Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory,” a Fifa spokesman told the Telegraph. “No employee at Uefa and Fifa has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino’s behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved.” Uefa confirmed a payment was made to the woman in question and that it covered the fees for her to complete an MBA course at a local business school. It said all payments were in line with regulations at the time, but those regulations have since been tightened and “reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organisation”. The claims put further pressure on Infantino, who is facing calls to resign as Fifa president over the World Cup private investment plan . The 56-year-old has apologised for “errors” he made in those controversial proposals, but did not step down after receiving the backing of senior executives in a meeting in Morocco on Wednesday. Infantino joined Uefa in 2000 and became secretary general in 2009, before being appointed Fifa president in 2016. European teams have threatened to boycott Fifa events despite the plans being aborted, saying certain conditions have not been met. But Conmebol – the South American confederation – and the Confederation of African Football (Caf) have backed Infantino, as have the football associations of World Cup co-hosts Mexico and tournament runners-up Argentina.

items.title: Sacked, Scattered, Waiting to Return — Untold story of Plateau’s communities emptied by violence
items.description: By Golok Nanmwa For decades, Plateau State was celebrated as Nigeria’s “Home of Peace and Tourism,” renowned for its breathtaking hills, fertile farmlands and rich cultural diversity. Communities across the state thrived on agriculture, commerce and peaceful coexistence. Read Also: 25 children from Kebbi, Kwara, Niger died in terrorists’ captivity — Lawmaker Today, that identity has been overshadowed by years of recurring violence that have left many rural communities deserted, thousands of residents displaced and vast stretches of farmland abandoned. Across Bokkos, Barkin Ladi, Riyom, Bassa, Mangu, Jos South, Kanam and Qua’an Pan Local Government Areas, villages that once echoed with children’s laughter, farming activities and bustling markets now bear the scars of repeated attacks. Homes have been razed, churches and schools destroyed, traditional institutions weakened and thousands of families forced into Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) camps or neighbouring communities. Governor Caleb Mutfwang recently acknowledged the magnitude of the crisis, disclosing during a television interview that several Plateau communities had been sacked by armed attackers. According to him, the objective of his administration is not merely to provide temporary humanitarian assistance but to ensure the safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced persons to their ancestral homes. That commitment reflects one of the most pressing humanitarian and security challenges confronting Plateau State today. Communities emptied by violence Although Plateau has experienced cycles of violence over the years, the attacks recorded in recent times have deepened the humanitarian crisis. Among the worst-hit local government areas are Bokkos, Barkin Ladi, Riyom, Bassa, Mangu, Jos South, Kanam and Qua’an Pan, where dozens of communities have suffered repeated attacks. Many displaced residents told Vanguard they have remained away from home for months because they fear fresh attacks and allege that some farmlands and surrounding areas remain occupied by armed groups. For farming families whose livelihoods depended entirely on agriculture, displacement has meant more than losing their homes. It has also meant losing their only source of income. Mary Pius, a displaced farmer now living in Heipang, Barkin Ladi Local Government Area, said life has become extremely difficult since she fled her community. “We have lost everything. Our farms are there, but we cannot go back because of fear. We only want peace so we can return home and begin farming again,” she said. Barkin Ladi: Communities living in fear Barkin Ladi remains one of Plateau’s major flashpoints. Communities around Ropp, Gashish, Fan, Heipang, Kakuruk, Mazat, Gwol, Fass, Jol, Sabon Layi and surrounding settlements have witnessed repeated attacks over the years. The July attack on Sabon Layi, where vigilante operatives were reportedly killed, heightened concerns over insecurity despite the deployment of security personnel. It could be recalled that a then serving Senator Gyang Dantong alongside a then member representing Barkin Ladi constituency Hon Gyang Fulani died after attending a mass burial in the local government in July 2012 .Indigenous youth organisations recently commended the Department of State Services (DSS) for establishing an operational base in the area, saying intelligence-driven operations had reduced attacks before fresh violence resurfaced. The groups alleged that criminal elements had adopted new tactics aimed at frustrating ongoing security operations. Riyom: “We only want to go home” Several communities have suffered attacks in Riyom local government. Communities including Kum, Wereng, Rim, Jol, Dyan, Bachi, Nding, Rakok and neighbouring villages have witnessed repeated attacks resulting in deaths, destruction of homes and fresh displacement. Some communities have also been taken over by these bandits. One of the latest attacks reportedly claimed the lives of a three-month-old baby alongside several other residents. Earlier attacks also claimed the lives of women, children and farmers returning from their farms. Barnabas Mathew, a youth leader in Riyom, said residents remain determined to return to their ancestral communities but insisted that security must first be guaranteed. “We have been sacked from our ancestral communities, but we still want to return home. Government must ensure adequate security. Our appeal is for security operatives to go after those occupying our communities so our people can safely return,” he said. He commended Governor Caleb Mutfwang for initiating plans to resettle displaced persons, saying the effort had restored hope to many victims. “We appreciate Governor Mutfwang’s commitment to returning displaced people to their ancestral homes. It is encouraging, but lasting peace will only come when those behind these attacks are flushed out completely.” Another community leader, Danlami Pam, also appealed for sustained military operations across vulnerable communities. “Our people have suffered enough. We are pleading with security agencies to pursue those responsible wherever they are hiding. Once security is guaranteed, our people are ready to return and rebuild their communities.” Residents insist that while humanitarian support has helped many displaced families survive, nothing compares to returning to their ancestral homes. They described displacement as a painful experience that has separated families, disrupted farming and deprived children of stable education. Bokkos: A community still mourning If any local government area symbolises the devastating human cost of Plateau’s insecurity, it is Bokkos. Once known for its thriving farming communities, the area has, over the years, witnessed repeated attacks that have left entire villages deserted, hundreds of families displaced and livelihoods destroyed. Communities including Hurti, Manguna, Daffo, Ruwi, Mbar, Tangur, Butura Kampani, Sha, Pyakmang, Darwat, Kopmur, Kawel, Mushere and Toff have all experienced varying degrees of violence, forcing thousands of residents to flee. Community leaders estimate that at least nine to 10 villages in Mushere District alone have been largely emptied following repeated attacks, leaving between 15,000 and 19,000 residents displaced. The humanitarian situation remains dire as many families continue to depend on assistance from government, churches, humanitarian organisations and kind-hearted individuals. The killing of the Saf Ron-Kulere of Bokkos, Late Lazarus Agaie, about a decade ago further underscored the deteriorating security situation in the area. The first-class traditional ruler was ambushed and killed by gunmen while returning from his farm in Sha District, an incident that shocked the state and renewed calls for stronger protection for traditional institutions. Several district heads, village heads and community leaders have also lost their lives in separate attacks over the years, leaving many communities without experienced leadership at a time they need it most. A clergyman, Mr. Henry Godfrey, said the people of Bokkos have endured enormous pain but remain hopeful that peace will return. “We have witnessed communities being completely wiped out. Families have been scattered while thousands now live in makeshift camps. What our people desire is not revenge but peace, justice and the opportunity to return home.” He lauded Governor Caleb Mutfwang’s determination to facilitate the return of displaced persons to their ancestral communities, describing the initiative as a major step towards restoring hope. According to him, rebuilding destroyed houses must go hand-in-hand with restoring security if displaced families are to return permanently. Bassa: Farmers abandon ancestral lands Bassa Local Government Area has also recorded repeated attacks over the years. Communities around Miango, Zike in Kwall District, Kimakpa, Kpachudu, Hwrra, Ta’agbe, Jebbu Miango, Ancha and Kperie have all suffered varying degrees of violence. Residents say fear has forced many farmers to abandon thousands of hectares of fertile agricultural land. For many households, farming was the only source of livelihood. Today, many displaced families depend almost entirely on humanitarian assistance and support from relatives. Community leaders warned that continued displacement could worsen food insecurity across Plateau State because many of the affected communities were major producers of maize, potatoes, vegetables and other food crops. Mangu and neighbouring communities Communities in Mangu Local Government Area have also experienced repeated attacks affecting settlements around Mangu Halle, Kombun, Fungzai, Chanso, Tyop, Sabon Gari and communities around the Panyam axis. Residents say attacks have displaced many families and placed enormous pressure on neighbouring communities receiving displaced persons. Many schools, health centres and places of worship have equally been affected by the insecurity. The state government has since directed that a comprehensive census be conducted in vulnerable communities as part of efforts to identify legitimate residents, prevent illegal occupation of abandoned settlements and prepare for future resettlement. Kanam and Qua’an Pan Communities in Kanam and Qua’an Pan Local Government Areas have also experienced attacks, kidnappings and killings. Residents say they now depend heavily on security patrols, the military and local vigilante groups to protect their communities. The killing of about 20 security personnel and vigilantes during an ambush in Garga area of Kanam further demonstrated the enormous risks faced by those protecting rural communities. Many residents insist that although security agencies have continued operations, more sustained action is needed to restore confidence among displaced families. The growing education crisis Beyond the destruction of homes and farmlands, insecurity is gradually undermining education across many rural communities. In Riyom and Barkin Ladi Local Government Areas particularly, repeated attacks have disrupted academic activities and forced temporary closure of several schools. Communities such as Shonong, Lwa, Fang, Bangai, Tanjol, Darwat, Daku-Jol and Hei-Gwe Kwi have all experienced disruptions affecting both primary and secondary schools. Similarly, Government Secondary School, Sho, Government Secondary School, Ropp and Dogo Primary School have all experienced interruptions resulting from insecurity. Parents say attacks or even rumours of attacks are enough to keep children and teachers away from school. Jennifer Dung, a parent from Riyom, said maintaining a stable academic calendar has become almost impossible. “Lessons are postponed, examinations rescheduled and children are constantly interrupted. Many of them now associate school with fear because they never know when another attack may occur,” she said. Danlami Pam, another resident, said prolonged school closures have left many children academically behind their counterparts in safer communities. According to him, some pupils now spend weeks out of school whenever attacks occur. Rwang Tenglong, spokesman of the Berom Youth Moulders, said meaningful educational development cannot take place where insecurity persists. “If our people are not secure, education cannot thrive. Government must first secure lives before children can concentrate on learning,” he said. Parents who can afford it have relocated to safer communities. Mrs. Kachllom Danlami, who moved from Ropp to Heipang with her family, said the decision was painful but necessary. “Because of the insecurity, I relocated. My child now attends school in Heipang without constant fear. Every parent wants that kind of peace.” For thousands of other displaced families, however, relocation remains financially impossible. They continue to hope that improved security will enable their children to return to schools within their ancestral communities. The human cost Beyond casualty figures lies an even greater tragedy. Thousands of children have had their education disrupted. Farmers have lost access to fertile lands. Women have lost husbands. Children have become orphans. Markets have collapsed. Healthcare facilities have either been destroyed or abandoned. Traditional rulers have become targets, while vigilante operatives and security personnel continue to pay the ultimate price defending vulnerable communities. Residents say rebuilding the Plateau will require far more than reconstructing houses. It will require rebuilding confidence, restoring livelihoods and ensuring that communities can once again live without fear. Government’s response: Returning IDPs to ancestral communities Recognising that military operations alone cannot solve the crisis, the Plateau State Government says it is pursuing a comprehensive strategy aimed at restoring displaced persons to their ancestral homes. Governor Caleb Mutfwang has repeatedly stated that the ultimate goal of his administration is not simply to provide temporary relief in Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) camps but to ensure the safe, voluntary and dignified return of victims to their communities. To actualise that vision, the government established a Resettlement Task Force chaired by retired Air Commodore Christopher Pam to develop a phased roadmap for returning displaced residents. The administration also received reports from the Land Administration Committee and the Resettlement Task Force to address issues surrounding land ownership, illegal occupation and the rebuilding of affected communities. As part of the initiative, the governor directed that a comprehensive census be conducted in vulnerable communities, particularly in parts of Mangu Local Government Area, to identify illegal occupants and prevent unauthorised settlements on lands abandoned by displaced residents. According to the governor, the exercise will assist the government in restoring legitimate owners to their ancestral communities while strengthening security around vulnerable settlements. The state government is also collaborating with the Federal Government, humanitarian organisations and development partners to mobilise resources for reconstruction and resettlement. Government said the programme includes the rebuilding of residential houses, schools, healthcare facilities and other critical infrastructure destroyed during attacks. The administration has equally strengthened collaboration with the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and other humanitarian agencies to support long-term recovery and community rebuilding. Governor Mutfwang maintains that rebuilding communities, restoring livelihoods and guaranteeing security remain central to his administration’s peace agenda. Communities affected Across Plateau State, many communities have either been attacked, destroyed or largely deserted following years of recurring violence. Among the affected communities are: Bokkos Local Government Area: Hurti, Manguna, Daffo, Ruwi, Maiyanga, Mbar, Tangur, Butura Kampani, Sha, Pyakmang, Darwat, Kopmur, Kawel, Mushere and Toff. Barkin Ladi Local Government Area: Gashish District communities, Heipang, Ropp, Dorowa Babuje, NTV, Kakuruk, Mazat, Lobiring, Fan, Tahoss, Marit and Dabwak. Riyom Local Government Area: Jol, Rim, Dyan, Wereng, Bachi, Gako, Sopp, Attakar, Razat and Hoss. Bassa Local Government Area: Zike in Kwall District, Kimakpa, Kpachudu, Hwrra, Ta’agbe, Miango axis communities, Jebbu Miango, Ancha and Kperie. Mangu Local Government Area: Mangu Halle, Sabon Gari, Pushit, Kerang, Kombun, Fungzai, Chanso, Tyop and communities around the Panyam axis. Other affected communities include Gero in Jos South Local Government Area, Rangarasa and Rantya in Jos South, Kwall District communities in Bassa, Nding Sesut community, Ngbra Zongo and Angwan Rukuba in Jos North. Residents said many of these communities have witnessed mass killings, destruction of homes, churches and food stores, occupation or abandonment of farmlands, displacement of thousands of residents and prolonged humanitarian hardship. A defining moment for Plateau For many displaced families, the dream remains simple: to return home. Across Bokkos, Barkin Ladi, Riyom, Bassa, Mangu, Jos South, Kanam and Qua’an Pan, thousands of families continue to hope that one day they will return to rebuild their homes, cultivate their farms and restore the peaceful lives they once knew. Mr Habila Rogo, a community leader in Bokkos who spoke to our correspondent said lasting peace will require sustained military operations, improved intelligence gathering, justice for victims, prosecution of perpetrators, reconstruction of destroyed infrastructure and expanded humanitarian support. He called on the federal government to tackle insecurity and ensure lasting peace in the state. Yet amid the pain, many residents remain hopeful. They say Governor Mutfwang’s commitment to returning displaced persons to their ancestral homes has renewed optimism, but stress that the success of the initiative will ultimately depend on sustained security operations, strong federal support, effective reconstruction and the political will to ensure that every displaced Plateau citizen can once again call home, home. Vanguard News The post Sacked, Scattered, Waiting to Return — Untold story of Plateau’s communities emptied by violence appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Économie russe : les drones ukrainiens font flamber l’exportation de brut
items.description: Selon des chiffres préliminaires publiés par S&P le 4 août, les exportations russes de produits pétroliers raffinés par voie maritime sont tombées à 1,18 million de barils par jour en juillet, contre 1,51 million en juin, soit leur niveau le plus bas depuis le début de la série en 2016 Russian oil product exports hit decade low in July amid Ukraine strikes », S&P, 4 août 2026.'> 1 . Cela est notamment dû aux frappes de drones ukrainiens qui ont mis hors service plus d'un tiers de la capacité de raffinage russe, faisant ainsi chuter les volumes traités à moins de 4 millions de barils par jour, soit le niveau le plus bas depuis plus de vingt ans. Mais si les exportations de produits raffinés s’effondrent, Moscou redirige vers l'export le brut qu'elle ne peut plus raffiner. Selon ces mêmes chiffres, les exportations maritimes de brut russe ont atteint 4,321 millions de barils par jour en juillet, soit une baisse de 7 % par rapport à juin, mais une hausse de 26 % par rapport à l'année précédente. Il s'agit également du deuxième meilleur résultat mensuel de l'année. Ainsi, si les frappes ukrainiennes touchent les capacités de raffinage et approchent la guerre des ménages russes, qui voient le prix de l’essence augmenter, elles libèrent dans le même temps des barils pour l’exportation. Fait à noter, les exportations vers la Chine atteignent 1,017 million de barils par jour, soit une hausse de 18 % sur un mois et de 12 % sur un an. Cela est cohérent avec le fait qu’en juillet, les importations chinoises de pétrole brut ont atteint leur plus haut niveau depuis trois mois Hormuz closure clouds China’s crude imports after they hit a 3-month high in July », 8 aout 2026.'> 2 . Pékin, premier importateur de pétrole transitant par le détroit d'Ormuz How China can survive without the Strait of Hormuz », Reuters , 1er avril 2026.'> 3 , a vu ses importations totales de brut chuter de 32 % au deuxième trimestre 2026, à 8,1 millions de barils par jour, un plus bas inédit depuis 2016 China’s crude oil imports fell in the second quarter, US Energy Information Administration », 31 juillet 2026.'> 4 . Les importations à destination de Singapour ont quant à elles augmenté de 112 % pour atteindre 456 000 barils par jour. Ce chiffre inclut les transbordements de navire à navire dans les eaux d'Asie du Sud-Est, une pratique en progression sous l'effet des sanctions occidentales, qui brouille la destination finale de ces barils. Si la Russie parvient donc à maintenir ses volumes d’exportation, elle perd en termes de recettes, le brut étant moins cher que les produits raffinés. Elle devient aussi de plus en plus dépendante de sa flotte fantôme, que le S&P estime désormais à environ 22 % de la flotte mondiale, soit un système de transport parallèle. L’article Économie russe : les drones ukrainiens font flamber l’exportation de brut est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Explainer: Why jobseekers are protesting results of a major civil service exam
items.description: Young people applying for entry-level jobs in Sindh’s bureaucracy have been protesting that only 70 out of over 4,300 of them have passed the exam held by the Sindh Public Service Commission. They sat ten written papers for the Combined Competitive Examination (CCE), whose shockingly slim number of successful candidates was announced on May 6. This is how assistant commissioners, assistant directors and section officers at Grades 16 and 17 are hired. Lower than 16 is for drivers and clerks hired in the districts. The highest grade is 22. Think chief secretary level. The SPSC typically passes at least five candidates per seat in its written examinations. However, according to spokesperson Hifzullah Kaka, that doesn’t necessarily apply to the CCE. Nevertheless, the 2024 results still struck protesters as impossible to accept. Alarm bells started ringing when the detailed marks certificates were uploaded after the results were announced. For instance, the 100-mark optional subject Criminology with a single exam paper was shown as two papers worth 200 marks in the detailed marks certificates. “At first, we thought it might be a mistake,” said Farman Ali, a candidate leading the campaign. “But it wasn’t limited to Criminology. We saw the same issue in Environmental Science as well.” SPSC spokesperson Kaka did not respond to a request for clarification and declined to comment, saying that the matter was in court. When Dawn visited the SPSC on August 5, guards did not permit entry. By May 7, the day after results were uploaded, social media was flooded with allegations of manipulation to pass a favoured few. That’s when the Sindh Students Action Committee got organised, according to one of the protestors, Wajahat Ahmed. A rally was held after which the protestors decided to keep up the pressure by refusing to move from outside the SPSC head office on Hyderabad’s Thandi Sarak. Protesters camp outside SPSC head office on Hyderabad’s Thandi Sarak. The backlash prompted the SPSC to lean on anti-terrorism laws. Among those it acted against was a US-based journalist and YouTuber, Imtiaz Chandio, who, along with two social media activists, Fayyaz Hussain Shar and Rafiullah Qureshi, was booked in a terrorism case for spreading “false propaganda and inciting” the candidates. SPSC Assistant Secretary Muhammad Mustafa registered an FIR at the GOR police station citing multiple sections of the Pakistan Penal Code, the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act and the Anti-Terrorism Act. On May 13, a rally drew students from across Sindh, who marched from Hyderabad’s Daudpota Library to Thandi Sarak. The next day, MQM-P lawmaker Maaz Mahboob submitted a resolution in the Sindh Assembly against the results, expressing “grave concern over the alleged irregularities, violations of merit and lack of transparency.” The resolution demanded that the disputed results be suspended immediately and an independent forensic audit of the examination process, marking system, and merit list be conducted by the Punjab Forensic Lab or any other impartial institution. On May 14, protesters launched the Movement for Restoration of Meritocracy, a broader campaign against what they describe as nepotism and the erosion of merit in public recruitment. Its name appears inspired by and rhymes with the famous Movement for the Restoration of Democracy, or MRD, launched in the 1980s to challenge the military regime. Its slogan claps back at the SPSC’s press release telling future candidates to sit the upcoming examinations with “zeal and zest”. So the MRM banners say, ‘Restore meritocracy with zeal and zest’, according to Farman Ali. He works as a grade 11 clerk at the Federal Board of Revenue. “Being a government employee, it is difficult to execute protests and raise a voice,” he said. “Since the intensity of injustice was high, I risked all that.” Banners and posters put up by protesting candidates outside the SPSC head office in Hyderabad. Landing in court The protests swelled, and students filed petitions challenging the results. A few days later, the Sindh High Court suspended them and summoned SPSC officials with the complete examination record. It said everything would be on hold. “According to the interim order, further appointments and proceedings based on the [CCE-24] results were halted,” Advocate Kamran Ali Isran, one of the lawyers representing the candidates, told Dawn . On May 22, the court extended the suspension till June 9 as the SPSC said that the record had been sealed in compliance with the court order. The court wanted the SPSC to explain how it addressed complaints that it was not being transparent. A month later, the court told a district and sessions judge to collect the examination record of the candidates who had failed CCE-24, seal it on the spot and bring it to the next hearing. In response, the SPSC went to the newly created Federal Constitutional Court to challenge the Sindh High Court’s orders through its lawyer Advocate Hafiz Ahsaan Ahmad Khokhar. It argued that the exam was held transparently, fairly and in line with the laws that applied: the Sindh Public Service Commission Act, 2022, and the Recruitment Management Regulations, 2023. By July 16, the federal court suspended the Sindh High Court’s interim orders for an inquiry, a stop to interviews of successful candidates and a recheck for failed candidates. With those orders lifted, the SPSC went ahead with interviewing the 70 successful candidates. As the hearings continue, so do the protests, which have spread to Nawabshah, Ghotki, Qambar, Umerkot, Islamkot, and Gambat. “In Sindh, wherever you go, knock on any door and ask, you will find someone who has been a victim of the SPSC,” says Zabiullah Mastoi, one of the participants in Hyderabad. SPSC head office on Hyderabad’s Thandi Sarak. According to journalist Imdad Soomro, who has covered SPSC for over a decade, the commission has long been a source of concern. “When I investigated it, I found that around 40 per cent of appointments were political, 40pc were made based on money, and only 20pc were on merit,” he claimed. “Gradually, merit came down to around 5pc, while the rest were political appointments or based on money.” Candidates who perform exceptionally well in the written examination are often eliminated at the interview stage, while those with lower written scores are given higher marks in the viva. The protesters say the court proceedings have done little to help. The camp continues, with candidates insisting they will stay until their demands are met: scrap the CCE-2024 and hold fresh exams, the chairman Muhammad Rizwan along with all commission members should resign, and an independent judicial commission should investigate SPSC examinations and recruitments for grades 16 and 17 over the past five years, among others. Header image: Protesters camp outside SPSC head office on Hyderabad’s Thandi Sarak. — All photos by Yumna Khan

items.title: Trump administration to invest $3 billion in minerals projects to boost US defence supply chains
items.description: The US government will invest $3 billion in critical minerals and battery projects as part of a push to increase domestic production and boost national security and industrial policy, US President Donald Trump said on Friday. “We’re reclaiming America’s rightful place as the minerals superpower of the world,” Trump told more than 200 mining executives, educators, investors and fellow politicians at a roundtable at the State Department aimed at supporting the industry, which he said had not received enough attention from Washington in recent years. He announced a slew of investments during his speech, including a $1.4bn conditional loan from the Defence Department’s Office of Strategic Capital for Sila Nanotechnologies, which makes lithium-ion battery parts. The OSC also extended a $400 million conditional loan to scandium miner Sunrise Energy Metals and a $150m conditional loan to magnet developer Niron Magnetics. The US Export-Import Bank will lend $58m to Westwater Resources, Global Advanced Metals and 5E Advanced Materials, which Reuters reported earlier on Friday. “Critical minerals are the raw materials of American strength that power everything from advanced weaponry to automobiles, and we want these essential products to be mined, refined and made right here in the USA,” Trump said. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and National Security Council official David Copley attended the announcement. Weapons stockpiles drive mineral demand The White House needs critical minerals to replenish weapons stockpiles depleted during the Iran conflict and reduce US dependence on Chinese supply chains. Several executives came with gifts for Trump. Tom Albanese, chairman of deep-sea mining firm American Ocean Minerals, gave Trump a gold replica of a nodule that the company hopes to mine from the Pacific seabed. Trump last year said he may bypass the UN-backed International Seabed Authority and issue international seabed mining licenses. Jim Litinsky, CEO of rare earths firm MP Materials, which is financially supported by the Pentagon, gave Trump magnets that had been produced for General Motors in the company’s Texas plant. Other attendees included executives from Lithium Americas , which is building the largest US lithium mine, NioCorp, which is building a scandium mine to supply defence contractor Lockheed Martin, and Energy Fuels , which received a $725m OSC conditional loan in June. US forces have burned through large numbers of precision-guided missiles and air-defence interceptors during the five-month-old US- Iran war. Defence officials and lawmakers have warned that replenishing some inventories could take years given existing production constraints. The Trump administration has disputed reports of significant shortages. Supplies of minerals including rare earths, tungsten, germanium and scandium are essential for manufacturing precision-guided missiles, fighter aircraft, armored vehicles, infrared sensors and other advanced weapons systems, according to Pentagon officials and defence companies. Mining schools receive funding boost The Department of Energy on Friday hosted representatives from all 14 accredited US mining schools to promote mining careers and encourage more students to enter the field. The department announced $100m in grants to help boost educational programs and set a goal of doubling the number of mining-related graduates at the nation’s universities within two years. “We need to work on some systemic changes to how we as a nation want to offer our brightest students an opportunity to participate in this industry,” said Assistant Energy Secretary Audrey Robertson. The Pentagon also said it would fund $80m in projects at three US mining schools. Officials have pointed to China’s extensive network of mining universities as a key advantage in its dominance of global mineral production. Since returning to office, Trump has launched a $12bn strategic minerals stockpile , backed equity investments in companies developing US mines and processing facilities, and sought to limit defence contractors’ reliance on supplies from China. The administration says government support is needed to counter decades of Chinese investment that left Beijing dominant in the mining and processing of many strategic minerals. Australia’s government on Saturday welcomed the Trump administration’s loan to Sunrise Energy Metals, which is developing a scandium mine in the country’s New South Wales state. “The Sunrise Scandium Project hosts the world’s largest and highest-grade known scandium resource, which has a range of vital aerospace, defence and clean energy applications,” Resources Minister Madeleine King said in a statement.

items.title: Vice President urges universities to embrace Artificial Intelligence
items.description: Vice President Professor Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang has urged universities across the country to embrace Artificial Intelligence (AI) by integrating digital literacy and emerging technologies into their academic programmes where necessary. Prof. Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang also called on universities to promote interdisciplinary research, support technology-based entrepreneurship and equip graduates to use Artificial Intelligence responsibly. The Vice President made the call at the 15th Graduation Ceremony of KAAF University, where 2,053 students graduated under the theme, “Transforming Lives, Transforming Ghana.” She encouraged the management of KAAF University to take advantage of Ghana’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy to equip graduates with the knowledge and skills required to navigate an increasingly technology-driven environment. Professor Opoku-Agyemang said KAAF University had demonstrated its commitment to producing graduates equipped with the knowledge, values and practical skills needed to succeed in a rapidly changing world. The Vice President also highlighted the “Teacher Dabre” initiative, which seeks to provide decent accommodation for teachers and address housing challenges, particularly for educators posted to rural communities. She said providing decent accommodation for teachers would help ensure that postings to rural communities did not become an additional hardship for educators. Meanwhile, Chancellor of KAAF University, Michael Aidoo, has appealed to the government to extend the ‘No Fees Stress’ initiative to students in private tertiary institutions. According to him, extending the initiative to students in private institutions would help reduce the financial burden on parents. He stressed that students attending private institutions are also Ghanaians and deserve government support.

Tinubu’s EFCC directive over Osun govt’s account sparks fresh questions over agency’s independence
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi, ABUJA President Bola Tinubu’s directive to the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission EFCC to vacate the court order freezing the Osun State government’s bank account has raised fresh questions about the anti-graft agency’s independence. Read Also: ‘I’m embarrassed by timing of EFCC action on Osun govt account – Tinubu Many Nigerians had taken to the social media to ask whether by fiat, the president can order the EFCC around, wondering whether the anti-graft’s agency inertia in the probes of former Humanitarian affairs Minister, Beta Edu and former Kogi state Governor, Yahaya Bello were due to presidential interference. Some of those who questioned the president’s action were the African Democratic Congress ADC, its presidential candidate Atiku Abubakar, and a Senior Advocate of Nigeria SAN all weighing in on the implications for the rule of law. The development followed Tinubu’s directive on Thursday ordering the EFCC to immediately return to court and vacate the order freezing the Osun government’s accounts. The president said although the commission acted within its statutory powers, the timing of the action — days before the August 15 governorship election — was inappropriate, adding that he felt “deeply embarrassed” by the development because actions of federal agencies are often attributed to the presidency. Before the president’s intervention, the EFCC had defended the freeze, with Wilson Uwujaren, the commission’s Director of Public Affairs, insisting the action was routine and not politically motivated. He cited a similar restriction placed on Edo State’s accounts before the 2024 governorship election, and said the commission could freeze an account for 72 hours without a court order, arguing it was still within the legal window. On the constitutional questions raised by the episode, Senior Advocate of Nigeria, Oba Maduabuchi, said the president does not have the power under any law to control the EFCC or the ICPC, but argued that public officers retain discretionary powers to act as they consider necessary in peculiar circumstances. “It would be wrong for us to hear that the person you are supposed to chase has powers to direct you how to chase him. And to do it publicly,” he said. He added that the president’s intervention, in his view, was “pardonable” given the risk that the freeze could be perceived as an attempt to influence the Osun election. Maduabuchi, however, faulted the manner of the president’s intervention, saying it ought to have been handled through the Attorney General rather than a public directive bearing the president’s personal signature. He also suggested that rather than freezing the entire Osun government account, the EFCC should have pursued the specific funds allegedly diverted to private companies. “Go after the money. Leave Oshun State. The one that is in the account is not missing. Go after the one that has left the account,” he said. The senior advocate that the episode reflected a broader problem of public trust, noting that unlike in other democracies, statements from Nigerian leaders on political and electoral matters are often met with public disbelief. “Nigerians do not trust their rulers,” he said. ADC National Publicity Secretary, Bolaji Abdullahi, had welcomed Tinubu’s directive but said the president’s explanation had raised more questions than answers, particularly around his reference to a court order authorising the account freeze. “What we find most curious about the statement is the President’s repeated reference to an alleged court order authorising the freezing of the Osun State Government’s accounts,” he said. Abdullahi noted that the EFCC had never publicly claimed to have obtained judicial approval before Tinubu’s intervention, defending its action instead on the basis of its statutory powers and what it described as its “preventive mandate.” He queried: “The obvious question, therefore, is: where did the President obtain the information that a court order existed? If such an order exists, why was it never mentioned by the EFCC in its statement while defending one of the most controversial actions it has taken in recent times?” He added that either the president was misinformed or had chosen to misrepresent the facts, describing both possibilities as “deeply disturbing.” In a separate statement issued by his Senior Special Assistant on Public Communication, Phrank Shaibu, Atiku Abubakar described the freezing of the account as a dangerous assault on democracy, insisting there could be no justification for it on the eve of a critical election. “It is impossible to ignore the implications of freezing a state’s principal operational account on the eve of a governorship election. Such an action could disrupt governance, delay salary payments, impede essential public services and create an atmosphere of intimidation that has no place in a democratic society,” he said. Atiku cautioned anti-corruption agencies against conduct that creates the perception they are being deployed to influence political outcomes, warning that “the selective and politically convenient deployment of state institutions diminishes public trust and weakens the democratic order.” He linked the development to what he called a pattern of coercive federal actions against opposition-controlled states, citing the earlier withholding of Osun State’s statutory local government allocations, and called on opposition parties and Nigerians committed to constitutional democracy to “close ranks and resist this dangerous drift before it is too late.” In a follow-up statement, Atiku challenged Tinubu to direct the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) to release former Kaduna State Governor Nasir El-Rufai, arguing that the president’s intervention in the Osun matter had demolished the long-held claim that anti-corruption agencies act independently of the presidency. “Having now demonstrated that he can issue direct operational directives to anti-corruption agencies whenever he considers it expedient, President Tinubu owes Nigerians an explanation as to why he cannot exercise the same authority in the case of Mallam Nasir El-Rufai,” he said. Atiku argued that the president could not simultaneously deny interference in EFCC operations while directing the commission’s next move, describing the arrangement as “executive control disguised as independence” rather than institutional autonomy. The post Tinubu’s EFCC directive over Osun govt’s account sparks fresh questions over agency’s independence appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Why Atiku is worried over strange payment into his bank account
items.description: By Emmanuel Aziken Fresh details have emerged on why former Vice President Atiku Abubakar is deeply concerned over a strange payment made into his personal bank account, with fears that the transaction could be part of an attempt to associate him with individuals or activities unknown to him. Read Also: Atiku raises alarm over mysterious credit alert, suspected data breach Saturday Vanguard gathered that beyond the unsolicited payment itself, concerns have arisen over the identity and possible motives of the sender, particularly against the backdrop of the description attached to the transaction: “Contribution Electioneering Campaign.” Atiku, through his spokesman, Phrank Shaibu, had raised the alarm after discovering the payment, insisting that neither the former Vice President nor his political organisation solicited or authorised it. “Neither His Excellency nor his campaign solicited, authorised or has any knowledge of the individual or entity behind the unauthorised payment,” Shaibu said in a statement. However, Saturday Vanguard gathered that one of the major concerns surrounding the transaction is the possibility that unsolicited funds could be used to create a financial trail linking the former Vice President to persons or activities with which he has no connection. There are fears within Atiku’s camp that unexplained payments could potentially expose the recipient to questions over links to terrorism financing, drug trafficking, fraud or other criminal activities, particularly where the true source and purpose of the funds remain unknown. There is, however, no evidence presently available to Saturday Vanguard that the money originated from any terrorist, drug trafficking or other criminal organisation. The concern is over the potential implications of receiving unexplained funds and the possibility that such transactions could subsequently be used to create damaging associations. How Did Sender Get Atiku’s Account Details? Another source of worry is how the sender obtained Atiku’s personal banking details in the first place. According to the earlier statement by Shaibu, the account into which the money was paid is strictly personal and its details are not publicly available. “The account is a strictly private one whose details are not in the public domain. This raises a fundamental question: How did unknown persons obtain the confidential banking details of a private citizen?” the statement said. Saturday Vanguard gathered that there are concerns that the account information, which may ordinarily be accessible to the bank and relevant financial regulatory institutions in the course of their statutory responsibilities, could have been improperly disclosed. Atiku’s camp has consequently raised questions over whether somebody with privileged access to sensitive financial information may have been responsible for exposing the details. “Even more disturbing is the suspicion that such confidential information may have been obtained through persons with privileged access,” the statement said. Bank Launches Investigation Saturday Vanguard gathered that the bank involved, one of Nigeria’s top five banks, has launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the transaction. The bank was expected to revert to Atiku with its findings at the weekend as efforts continued to establish how the transaction occurred and, crucially, whether it could help identify its origin. Further checks by Saturday Vanguard indicated that the money was transferred from an OPay account, potentially adding another layer to efforts to establish the identity behind the payment. While transactions conducted through regulated financial platforms ordinarily leave records that may assist investigations, Atiku’s concern remains that the person immediately associated with the transfer may not necessarily reveal who ultimately initiated or motivated it. Wider Security Concerns The former Vice President believes the implications extend beyond his personal circumstances. “If the private banking information of a former Vice President and a leading presidential candidate can be accessed and deployed for reasons yet unknown then no Nigerian’s financial privacy is safe,” the statement quoted him as saying. Atiku also warned that unauthorised access to confidential financial information could create potentially serious security vulnerabilities for ordinary Nigerians. “If established, this would amount to a grave abuse of power capable of exposing the account holder to kidnappers, terrorists, bandits, fraudsters and other criminal elements,” the statement added. For Atiku, therefore, the mystery is not simply about money unexpectedly appearing in his account. The questions are who sent it, why it was labelled an electioneering campaign contribution, how the sender obtained details of a private account and what purpose the transaction was intended to serve. Those questions have assumed greater significance given Atiku’s status as a former Vice President and prominent opposition politician ahead of the 2027 general elections. According to his spokesman, the matter has already been brought to the attention of security agencies and the Nigerian public. His camp views the development as one of a number of suspicious incidents in the political environment ahead of 2027 and wants the source of the payment, as well as how the sender obtained the account details, conclusively established. Until those questions are answered, the strange deposit is being treated not as a windfall but as a potential security and political red flag. items.title: STU Lecture Equips Researchers with Strategies for Stronger Academic Papers
items.description: The Directorate of Grants, Research and Development (DGRD) of the Sunyani Technical University (STU) has organised a public lecture to equip researchers and students with practical strategies for producing quality academic papers. The lecture, on the theme “The Anatomy of a Strong Academic Paper in Management Studies”, was delivered by Professor Samuel Adomako, Professor of Entrepreneurship and Innovation at the University of Birmingham, United Kingdom. Prof. Adomako stressed the importance of precision, relevance and originality in academic writing, urging researchers to ensure their work makes a meaningful contribution to knowledge. He advised researchers to write abstracts after completing their studies, saying an abstract should concisely capture the research gap, objectives, methodology, findings and theoretical contribution. On writing introductions, Prof. Adomako said the opening paragraph should immediately engage readers and establish the significance of the study. He urged researchers to identify clear research gaps and frame their studies around compelling research puzzles. He also cautioned against vague problem statements and encouraged researchers to engage with recent literature to ensure their studies address contemporary academic issues. On theory and hypotheses, he stressed the need to select appropriate theories to guide research, describing a hypothesis as “a bridge between theory and research”. Prof. Adomako further advised researchers to clearly explain their data, samples, variables and measurement techniques in the methodology section while identifying and addressing potential biases. For the results section, he urged researchers to present their findings clearly without unnecessarily linking them to existing literature. He also cautioned against copying raw statistical outputs directly into academic papers. In discussing the final section, he recommended that researchers restate the purpose of their study, interpret the findings and clearly articulate their theoretical contribution. He also encouraged researchers to examine the limitations and suggested future research directions of previous studies as a way of identifying opportunities for further research. The Acting Pro-Vice Chancellor of STU, Prof. Evans Zoya Kpamma, supported the call for impactful research, stressing that academics should focus on contributing to knowledge rather than publishing solely for career advancement. “We should not just be publishing for promotion’s sake, but by contributing to knowledge,” he said. Earlier, the Director of Grants, Research and Development, Prof. Edward Owusu, said the lecture formed part of the university’s efforts to strengthen research capacity, promote intellectual discourse and advance academic excellence.

Saidu Baba-Ahmed disclosed this yesterday while speaking on the conditions of the 315 kidnap victims who regained their freedom on Thursday night after spending six months in captivity. The figure comprises 308 victims rescued from terrorist captivity in the forests of Kwara and Niger states and seven students of Gateway ICT Polytechnic, Saapade in Ogun state who were abducted last week. The lawmaker, in an interview told Saturday Vanguard that 12 of the youths joined the terrorists’ army and were not among those released by the terrorists. According to him, “The terrorists asked the youths who among them would like to join their army and 12 of them volunteered to join them. So, those youths are not among those who were released. “25 children from Kebbi, Niger and Kwara states also died in captivity and some died in transit and they were buried there. A total of 176 victims were kidnapped from Kwara state and 163 regained their freedom. 15 of the victims are still missing now. “Also, none of the women came with pregnancy but two women who were kidnapped with pregnancy came back with two babies. We checked them properly and discovered that none of them is pregnant, because they told us that their abductors didn’t touch them. But two women who were abducted with pregnancy came back with two babies“. Hon. Saidu Baba-Ahmed said that those who were set free arrived in Ilorin, the Kwara state capital and 46 of them were receiving medical attention at the hospital. He also said that the state government was taking care of them to ascertain their state of health before reuniting them with their families. The lawmaker then commended the state and the federal governments for their efforts in ensuring that the abductees returned home safely. The victims who were abducted during the deadly attack on Woro community in Kaiama Local Government Area of Kwara State were received at the Nigerian Army’s 2 Division, Sobi Barracks, Ilorin before being moved to an undisclosed location where they spent the night. The victims were kidnapped when armed terrorists invaded the community on February 3 this year, killing scores of residents and whisking away the victims into the forest, triggering widespread outrage and intensified security operations. Following sustained military operations and coordinated efforts by security agencies, the victims regained their freedom and were transported from Niger State to Ilorin late Thursday night. The rescued victims were expected to be officially handed over to Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, who has consistently engaged security authorities to ensure their safe return. Their arrival marks a major breakthrough in the months-long efforts to secure the release of the abductees, while authorities continue to verify the number of those rescued and provide necessary care and support. Meanwhile, Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq of Kwara state while receiving the victims of Woro attack in Ilorin yesterday described the February bloody event as not only sad, but regrettable. The governor received the victims who are mostly kids and women, from the 22 Armoured Brigade Commander Brigadier General Nicholas Rume. Mallam AbdulRazaq also hailed President Bola Tinubu for his swift response and assistance to the state. He added that the president had approved the establishment of five Army Battalions in Omu-Aran, Patigi, Ilemona, Kosubosu and Kaiama. items.title: Captain martyred, 7 terrorists killed in intelligence-based operation in Hangu: ISPR
items.description: The military media affairs wing said on Saturday that a captain was martyred while seven terrorists were killed during an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Hangu district. In a statement, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said security forces conducted an IBO in Hangu on Friday following reports about the presence of terrorists belonging to Fitna al Khawarij — a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan. During the operation, troops effectively engaged the terrorists, it said. “In desperation, the khawarij took refuge inside a mosque, blatantly disregarding the sanctity of the place of worship. In ensuing fire exchange, seven khawarij , belonging to Indian-sponsored Fitna al Khawarij were sent to hell,” it said. The statement went on to say that during the exchange of fire, 27-year-old Captain Hamza Akram, a resident of Punjab’s Narowal district who was “leading his troops from front and relentlessly pursuing” the terrorists, embraced martyrdom. “Weapons and ammunition were also recovered from the killed khawarij , who remained actively involved in numerous terrorist activities against the security forces and law enforcement agencies as well as killing of innocent civilians,” it said. ISPR said that a sanitisation operation was being conducted to eliminate any other Indian-sponsored terrorists in the area. President Asif Ali Zardari paid tribute to the martyred captain saying, “The motherland pays its profound tribute to the great sacrifice of its brave son.” “The entire nation is indebted to the eternal sacrifices of these brave sons for the motherland,” the president added, offering prayers for the bereaved family. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi paid tribute to the martyred captain and offered his condolences to the bereaved family. He said that the martyred officer had paid the ultimate sacrifice for the homeland and would remain alive in our hearts. A day earlier, ISPR said 10 terrorists were killed in two separate engagements in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It said that in the first encounter, a group of terrorists attempted to attack security forces’ checkposts in Azam Warsak area in South Waziristan, which was effectively thwarted, resulting in the deaths of eight terrorists. “In another encounter that took place in Dir district, own troops successfully neutralised two more khawarij ,” it added. Terrorist commander killed in Bannu Separately, security forces killed a key terrorist commander, identified as Jamidullah, during an operation in Jani Khel area of KP’s Bannu district, a security official said. The official said that the terrorist commander was involved in terrorist activities and was considered a quadcopter expert. The official said that security forces conducted the operation in Jani Khel on the basis of intelligence reports, during which Jamidullah was targeted and killed. According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies , an Islamabad-based think tank, violence linked to terrorist attacks and counter-terrorism operations intensified sharply in July, making it the deadliest month of 2026, with 112 security personnel among 205 people killed.
